I have the complete picture now. Here's the full trace. ## The holding spot: "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRNB) ERPNext parks the value of received-but-unbilled goods in a **liability account** — `Stock Received But Not Billed` (for fixed-asset receipts, the parallel `Asset Received But Not Billed`). It's a Company-level default field, provisioned at company creation only when perpetual inventory is enabled (`erpnext/setup/doctype/company/company.py:701-708`), and sits under *Current Liabilities → Stock Liabilities* in the standard chart of accounts with `account_type: "Stock Received But Not Billed"` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/account/chart_of_accounts/verified/standard_chart_of_accounts.py:164-168`). It's effectively an "amount we owe the supplier for goods already taken in" placeholder. ## Receipt side — value parked in SRNB 1. **`PurchaseReceipt.on_submit`** (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/purchase_receipt.py:363`) → `self.make_gl_entries()` (line 383), inherited from **`StockController.make_gl_entries`** (`erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py:178`). That method builds the `inventory_account_map` (warehouse → inventory account) and calls the PR-specific `get_gl_entries` (`purchase_receipt.py:478`). 2. **`PurchaseReceiptGLComposer.compose`** (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py:23`) builds the voucher's GL entries, then hands them to `process_gl_map` in `erpnext/accounts/general_ledger.py`. The item loop is in **`_make_item_gl_entries`** (line 39). For each stock item under perpetual inventory: - `stock_asset_rbnb = doc.get_company_default("stock_received_but_not_billed")` (lines 297–301); - **`make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry`** (line 57, invoked line 329): **Dr** the warehouse's inventory account for `get_stock_value_difference(doc.name, d.name, d.warehouse)` — the goods now sit in Stock; - **`make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry`** (line 74, invoked line 330): **Cr** the SRNB account by the item's `base_net_amount` (posted as a negative debit with `against_account` = the stock account). It also carries the exchange-rate-discrepancy adjustments when the invoice already exists (lines 126–162). 3. Surrounding helpers credit/carry the rest of the landed value against the same SRNB: valuation taxes (`_make_tax_gl_entries`, line 394), landed-cost amounts (`make_landed_cost_gl_entries`), sub-contracting cost, and any purchase-price variance via `get_divisional_loss_account` (line 370, PPV account for Standard-Cost items). **Net result on receipt:** Dr Stock (asset) / Cr Stock Received But Not Billed. The value of the goods is on the balance sheet, but there's no supplier payable yet — the credit "parks" it in SRNB. ## Billing side — value moves out of SRNB when the bill arrives 1. **At validation** — `PurchaseInvoice.validate` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/purchase_invoice.py:257`) calls **`ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account(for_validate=True)`** (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:20`). This is the crucial redirection: for stock items (perpetual inventory on, non-opening, not fixed asset, not drop-ship), if the row is linked to a receipt (`item.purchase_receipt`), it checks whether SRNB was actually credited in that PR (`frappe.db.exists("GL Entry", {voucher_type: "Purchase Receipt", voucher_no: ..., account: stock_not_billed_account})`, lines 57–65) and then **forces `item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account`** (line 82), msgprint-ing "Expense Head changed…" if the user chose something else. If no PR exists yet, it does the same with the rationale "PI created before PR" (lines 83–102). Fixed-asset items get the identical treatment with `asset_received_but_not_billed` (lines 120–137). `set_against_expense_account` (line 164) records SRNB as the invoice's `against_expense_account`. 2. **At submission** — `PurchaseInvoice.on_submit` (line 607) → `self.make_gl_entries()` (line 639) → **`PurchaseInvoice.make_gl_entries`** (line 671) → `get_gl_entries` (line 703) → **`PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.compose`** (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:18`), which: - **`make_supplier_gl_entry`** (line 80): **Cr** `doc.credit_to` (Creditors / Accounts Payable) for the grand total — the genuine liability is born here, "against" the SRNB account; - **`make_item_gl_entries`** (line 129): in the no-`update_stock` branch (lines 319–350), **Dr** `item.expense_account` — which `set_expense_account` has pointed at SRNB — for the full billed amount. The in-code comment (lines 332–336) states it outright: *the invoice has no stock impact; the linked PR already booked the stock and the PPV, so here we only clear "Stock Received But Not Billed" at the full billed amount against the supplier* (re-booking the variance would double-count and leave SRNB partially uncleared); - **Tax symmetry** — `compose` line 26 loads `doc.stock_received_but_not_billed`; `make_item_gl_entries` (lines 395–439) checks whether the PR booked valuation taxes against SRNB. If it did **not** (e.g., taxes only appear on the bill), the invoice **Dr SRNB / Cr valuation tax accounts** ("Post reverse entry for Stock-Received-But-Not-Billed", `make_tax_gl_entries` lines 650–680) so the liability isn't stranded. 3. Operationally, `BillingStatusService.update_billing_status_in_pr()` (called in `on_submit`, line 629) raises the PR's `billed_amt`/`per_billed`, and `BillingValidationService.validate_multiple_billing("Purchase Receipt", "pr_detail", "amount")` (validate, line 297) prevents over-billing a receipt row. ## Net effect and variants - PR alone: Dr Stock / Cr **SRNB** → SRNB shows an open credit while goods await the bill. - PI against PR: Dr **SRNB** / Cr Creditors → the SRNB credit and debit offset to zero, leaving the durable state **Dr Stock, Cr Creditors**. Partial billing just clears SRNB proportionally. - Reverse order (bill first, goods later): the invoice still debits SRNB (no PR link, expense_account.py line 102), and the later PR's composer credits it — the `item.purchase_invoice` branch in `make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry` handles the resulting exchange-rate discrepancy. - `update_stock` invoices (goods received on the bill itself) never park anything: `set_expense_account` points the debit straight at the warehouse inventory account (expense_account.py lines 51–54). - The parked amounts are inspectable per document via the **"Received Items To Be Billed"** (`erpnext/accounts/report/received_items_to_be_billed`) and **"Billed Items To Be Received"** (`erpnext/accounts/report/billed_items_to_be_received`) reports.

## The holding spot: the **"Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB)** account ERPNext parks the value of received-but-unbilled goods in a temporary liability account set as a Company default (`stock_received_but_not_billed`, auto-created as "Stock Received But Not Billed" in `erpnext/setup/doctype/company/company.py:704`; fixed assets have the parallel `asset_received_but_not_billed`). The whole mechanism only runs under perpetual inventory (`erpnext.is_perpetual_inventory_enabled(company)` — the gate in `StockController.make_gl_entries`). ## Receipt side — value parked on PR submit 1. **`PurchaseReceipt.on_submit`** (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/purchase_receipt.py:363`) → `update_stock_ledger()` (goods into warehouse) → `self.make_gl_entries()` (line 383). 2. `make_gl_entries` resolves via the class chain `PurchaseReceipt → BuyingController → SubcontractingController → **StockController.make_gl_entries**` (`erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py:178`), which calls the PR override `PurchaseReceipt.get_gl_entries` (`purchase_receipt.py:478`) → **`PurchaseReceiptGLComposer.compose`** (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py:23`). 3. In `_make_item_gl_entries`, per stock item, for each item where perpetual inventory is on (lines 290–335), `stock_asset_rbnb = doc.get_company_default("stock_received_but_not_billed")` (line 297–301), then two paired entries: - **`make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry`** (line 57) — **Dr Stock/Inventory account** (the warehouse's account from `get_inventory_account_dict`, amount = `get_stock_value_difference`), `against_account = stock_asset_rbnb`. - **`make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry`** (line 74) — **Cr Stock Received But Not Billed** for `item.base_net_amount` (posted as a negative debit), except on internal transfers, where the credit goes to the from-warehouse account instead. Net entry: **Dr Inventory / Cr Stock Received But Not Billed**. Because there's no supplier bill yet, the credit lands in SRBNB — not Accounts Payable. (Valuation-category taxes are similarly parked via `_make_tax_gl_entries`/`negative_expense_to_be_booked`.) ## Billing side — value flushed out when the bill arrives 1. **`PurchaseInvoice.set_expense_account`** (`purchase_invoice.py:450`) → **`ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account`** (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:20`). For each stock item (not opening/drop-ship/fixed-asset): - With **Update Stock** ticked: `item.expense_account` = the warehouse inventory account (lines 51–54) — the PI books its own receipt, SRBNB isn't involved. - Normal case (billing an existing PR): it looks up whether the PR actually credited SRBNB — `frappe.db.exists("GL Entry", {voucher_type: "Purchase Receipt", voucher_no: item.purchase_receipt, account: stock_not_billed_account})` (lines 57–65) — and if so forces **`item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account`** (line 82). If no PR exists yet, it also uses SRBNB (lines 84–102), so PR-after-PI still nets correctly. 2. **`PurchaseInvoice.on_submit`** (`purchase_invoice.py:607`): stock ledger is touched only when `update_stock == 1` (line 636); then `self.make_gl_entries()` unconditionally (line 639) → `get_gl_entries` → **`PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.compose`** (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:18`), which re-reads `doc.stock_received_but_not_billed = doc.get_company_default(...)` (line 26). 3. Inside `compose`: - **`make_supplier_gl_entry`** — **Cr supplier's `credit_to`** (Accounts Payable) for the grand total. - **`make_item_gl_entries`** (line 129), non-update-stock path (lines 331–350): **Dr `expense_account` (= SRBNB) against the supplier** for the billed amount. The in-code comment says it directly: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock … Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier."* No second stock debit, so the inventory account isn't double-counted. - Exchange-rate drift vs. the PR is booked as an extra Dr to SRBNB + Cr to `exchange_gain_loss_account` (lines 352–393, mirrored on the PR side at `gl_composer.py:126–162`). - If the PR never booked the valuation taxes, the PI debits SRBNB for `item_tax_amount` and accumulates `doc.negative_expense_to_be_booked` ("Post reverse entry for Stock-Received-But-Not-Billed if booked in Purchase Receipt", lines 395–439), which `doc.set_gl_entry_for_purchase_expense` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:354`) then routes to the real expense accounts. Net entry on billing: **Dr Stock Received But Not Billed / Cr Accounts Payable** — the parked credit is cleared, and the liability finally sits with the supplier. (Operational status like `per_billed` is updated separately by the `BillingStatusService` in each doctype's `services/billing_status.py`, but the ledger movement is entirely the GL pair above.)

## Answer At save time, ERPNext runs a dedicated server-side validation that rejects a Pricing Rule containing both an item template and one of that template's own variants. Here's the full chain: ### Where it lives All of it is in the Pricing Rule doctype controller: **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/pricing_rule.py`** (class `PricingRule(Document)`). There is **no client-side counterpart** — `pricing_rule.js` contains no variant/validate logic, so the check fires purely on the server during `frappe`'s document `validate()` hook (i.e., on both insert and subsequent saves). ### Call chain 1. **`PricingRule.validate()`** (line 130) — invoked on every save; it calls `validate_duplicate_apply_on()`. 2. **`validate_duplicate_apply_on()`** (line 148) — since `apply_on != "Transaction"`, it resolves the child table from the module-level map `apply_on_dict = {"Item Code": "items", "Item Group": "item_groups", "Brand": "brands"}`. For `apply_on == "Item Code"` the child table is `items` (child doctype **`PricingRuleItemCode`**, which has a single `item_code` Link field plus `uom`). It then: - **Duplicate check first:** collects `values = [d.get("item_code") for d in self.items if d.get("item_code")]` and throws `"Duplicate Item Code found in the table"` if `len(values) != len(set(values))` (exact-duplicate rows only). - **Template/variant check next:** because `apply_on == "Item Code"` (line 159–160), it calls `self.validate_template_with_variant(values)`. 3. **`validate_template_with_variant(item_codes)`** (line 162) — the specific check you're asking about. It runs a single query against the Item doctype: ```python variants = frappe.get_all( "Item", filters={"name": ("in", item_codes), "variant_of": ("in", item_codes)}, fields=["name", "variant_of"], ) ``` This uses the Item master's **`variant_of`** field (the Link from a variant back to its template). The `IN ... IN` double filter matches any item whose *name* is in the rule's item list **and** whose *template* (`variant_of`) is **also** in that same list — i.e., it detects the exact "template + its own child variant both selected" conflict, not just any two related items. 4. If the query returns rows, it throws (raising `frappe.ValidationError`, which aborts the save): > **"Variant {0} and its template {1} cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule"** with the variant name and template name bolded via `frappe.bold()`. ### Behavior nuances - Only the **first** offending pair is reported (`variants[0]`), even if multiple conflicts exist. - The check is strictly **template vs. its own direct variant**. Adding two different variants of the same template, or a template plus an unrelated variant, passes validation. - It applies only when `apply_on == "Item Code"`; "Item Group" and "Brand" modes only get the duplicate-value check. ### Test confirming the behavior **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/test_pricing_rule.py::test_pricing_rule_with_template_and_its_variant`** (line 336): it creates variant `Test Variant PRT` (with `variant_of = "_Test Variant Item"`), appends both `"_Test Variant Item"` and `"Test Variant PRT"` to `rule.items`, and asserts `self.assertRaises(frappe.ValidationError, rule.insert)` — i.e., `rule.insert()` fails precisely because of `validate_template_with_variant`.

## Answer Yes — a dedicated save-time validation catches exactly this case and rejects the document. ### Where it runs `erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/pricing_rule.py`: 1. **`PricingRule.validate()`** (line 130) — the standard Frappe `validate` hook, executed on every save — calls **`self.validate_duplicate_apply_on()`** as its second step (line 132). 2. **`validate_duplicate_apply_on()`** (lines 148–160): since `self.apply_on != "Transaction"`, it resolves the child table from the module-level mapping `apply_on_dict = {"Item Code": "items", "Item Group": "item_groups", "Brand": "brands"}` (line 15). For `"Item Code"` that's the `items` table (`Pricing Rule Item Code`). It collects `d.get("item_code")` from every row (`frappe.scrub("Item Code")` → `"item_code"`). A template and its variant are different item codes, so the plain duplicate check (`Duplicate {0} found in the table`, line 156–157) passes — then, because `apply_on == "Item Code"`, it calls **`validate_template_with_variant(values)`** (line 159–160). 3. **`validate_template_with_variant(item_codes)`** (lines 162–175) — this is the actual detection. ### What it specifically checks It issues a single query against the Item doctype using both filters over the *same* submitted list of codes: ```python variants = frappe.get_all( "Item", filters={"name": ("in", item_codes), "variant_of": ("in", item_codes)}, fields=["name", "variant_of"], ) ``` In other words: it finds any item in the rule's item list whose **`variant_of`** (the link each variant holds to its parent template) is *also* present in that same list. If the user added template `T` and one of its variants `V` (where `V.variant_of == T`), row `V` satisfies both conditions and is returned. If any row matches, it throws and blocks the save, naming the first offending pair found: > **"Variant V and its template T cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule"** (with `frappe.bold` on both names). ### Scope and rationale - The check is pairwise-within-one-rule only: two *variants* of the same template, or a template + variant in *two different* rules, are not rejected. It also only applies to `apply_on == "Item Code"` (not Item Group/Brand/Transaction). - The reason this validation exists is visible in the matching engine, `erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/utils.py::_get_pricing_rules` (lines 114–126): at apply time, when a transaction line has a variant item, the query adds `item_variant_condition = " or {child_doc}.item_code=%(variant_of)s"`, so a rule written for the template would also match the variant — which is exactly why allowing both the template and its variant in one rule would create an ambiguous/conflicting match.

## Answer Yes — a dedicated save-time validation catches exactly this case, and it rejects the document with a `frappe.ValidationError`. ### Where it runs `PricingRule.validate()` in **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/pricing_rule.py`** (line 130) is the standard Frappe `Document` hook that fires on every insert/save. Its second step (line 132) is `validate_duplicate_apply_on()`: ```python apply_on_dict = {"Item Code": "items", "Item Group": "item_groups", "Brand": "brands"} ``` For `apply_on == "Item Code"`, the relevant child table is **Pricing Rule Item Code** (`items`, docclass `PricingRuleItemCode` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule_item_code/pricing_rule_item_code.py`). ### What it checks, step by step **1. `validate_duplicate_apply_on()` (lines 148–160):** - Collects all non-empty `item_code` values from the `items` child table. - First throws `"Duplicate {0} found in the table"` if the same code appears twice. - Then, specifically because `self.apply_on == "Item Code"` (line 159), calls the template/variant check. **2. `validate_template_with_variant(item_codes)` (lines 162–175) — the check that catches your scenario:** ```python variants = frappe.get_all( "Item", filters={"name": ("in", item_codes), "variant_of": ("in", item_codes)}, fields=["name", "variant_of"], ) if variants: variant = variants[0] frappe.throw( _("Variant {0} and its template {1} cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule").format(...) ) ``` It runs a **single query against the `Item` doctype** with two `IN` clauses over the same list of codes from the rule's item table: - `name in item_codes` — the row is one of the items on the rule, **and** - `variant_of in item_codes` — that item's template link (`variant_of`) also points to an item on the same rule. In other words, it detects whether any listed item is a variant whose direct parent template is *also* listed on the same Pricing Rule. If such a pair exists, `frappe.throw()` aborts the save with: > *"Variant **{variant}** and its template **{template}** cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule"* Only the first offending pair (`variants[0]`) is reported, and it checks the direct `variant_of` link (one level — the template/variant hierarchy in ERPNext is only one level deep anyway). ### Behavior notes - This fires only for `apply_on = "Item Code"`; "Item Group", "Brand" get only the plain duplicate check, and `"Transaction"` short-circuits out entirely (line 149). - It's a save-time (validate hook) check on the Pricing Rule doc itself — it does not prevent the *Item* records from existing, only the conflicting rule configuration. ### Regression test `test_pricing_rule_with_template_and_its_variant` in **`erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/test_pricing_rule.py`** (line 336) covers exactly this: it appends the template `_Test Variant Item` and its variant `Test Variant PRT` (whose `variant_of` is the template) to one rule's `items` table, and asserts `self.assertRaises(frappe.ValidationError, rule.insert)`.

Yes — a validation runs and the save is **rejected**. Here is the full, specific picture (all in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/pricing_rule.py`): ## Call chain at save time `PricingRule.validate()` (line 130) → `self.validate_duplicate_apply_on()` (line 132) → `self.validate_template_with_variant(values)` (line 160). ## Step 1 — `validate_duplicate_apply_on()` (lines 148–160) Since `apply_on == "Item Code"` (not `"Transaction"`): 1. It resolves the child table via the module-level map (line 15): `apply_on_dict = {"Item Code": "items", "Item Group": "item_groups", "Brand": "brands"}` → for Item Code, the child table is **`items`** (rows of doctype `PricingRuleItemCode`). 2. `apply_on_field = frappe.scrub(self.apply_on)` → `"item_code"`. It then collects every non-empty `item_code` from the `items` rows: `values = [d.get(apply_on_field) for d in self.get(apply_on_table) if d.get(apply_on_field)]`. 3. A preliminary duplicate check: `if len(values) != len(set(values))` → throws `"Duplicate Item Code found in the table"` (this catches literally the same item listed twice — not your scenario, but it runs first). 4. Because `apply_on == "Item Code"`, it passes the collected `values` (the whole item list) into `validate_template_with_variant(values)`. ## Step 2 — `validate_template_with_variant()` (lines 162–175): the template-vs-variant check This is what specifically catches your scenario. It issues **one self-referential query** against the Item doctype: ```python variants = frappe.get_all( "Item", filters={"name": ("in", item_codes), "variant_of": ("in", item_codes)}, fields=["name", "variant_of"], ) ``` How the detection works: on the Item doctype, every variant carries a **`variant_of` link field** pointing at its parent template (the template itself has `has_variants` and does not point back). So the query asks a single question with two `IN` clauses against the *same* list of item codes selected in the rule: - `name ∈ item_codes` — the item itself is in the rule's item list, **and** - `variant_of ∈ item_codes` — the item's parent **template is also in that same list**. If any row matches (i.e., a variant whose template is simultaneously listed), the method throws and aborts the save: ```python if variants: variant = variants[0] frappe.throw( _("Variant {0} and its template {1} cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule").format( frappe.bold(variant.name), frappe.bold(variant.variant_of) ) ) ``` The user sees a validation error like: "**Variant VAR-XXX and its template TPL-YYY cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule**", and the Pricing Rule document is not saved. ## Notable details - The check is bidirectional-by-construction: because the variant→template relationship lives only on the variant side (`variant_of`), one query suffices regardless of the order in which the template and variant rows appear in the `items` child table. - It reports only the **first** conflicting pair (`variants[0]`); if multiple template/variant pairs conflict, fixing one and re-saving surfaces the next. - It only fires when a template **and its own direct variant** coexist in one rule. Two sibling variants of the same template (template not listed), or a template listed alone, pass fine. It's also scoped per single Pricing Rule — a template in one rule and its variant in another rule is allowed. - These two methods are the only definitions and callers of this check in the codebase (confirmed by grep) — the logic lives entirely inside the `PricingRule` controller's `validate()` hook, so it executes on both document insert and every subsequent save/update.

## Short answer ERPNext never relies on `posting_datetime` alone. The stock ledger's total ordering is the composite key **`(posting_datetime, creation)`** — `posting_datetime` is the user‑chosen date+time, and `creation` (the row's insert timestamp, shared by all SLE rows of one voucher submission) is the deterministic tie‑breaker for entries that share the exact same second. Every "previous vs. current vs. future" decision during reposting — including the cancel path — is expressed against that pair, so a same‑second Purchase Receipt + Material Transfer have a well‑defined order, and cancelling one of them re‑anchors and re‑runs the surviving same‑second entry instead of trusting the old balances. ## Where the ordering is defined All in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` unless noted: 1. **Canonical query ordering** — `get_stock_ledger_entries()` (line ~2065) ends with `order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}` (line 2071). It backs `get_previous_sle()` (`<=`, desc, limit 1), `get_sle_before_datetime()`, `get_sle_after_datetime()` and `get_future_entries_to_repost()` (`>=`, asc). 2. **Repost‑queue ordering** — `update_entries_after.sort_sles()` (lines 803–810) sorts every SLE to be reposted by `(get_datetime(posting_datetime), get_datetime(creation))`; `repost_stock_ledgers()` pops them from a deque in that order and chains balances via `self.prev_sle_dict[key] = sle` after each `process_sle()` (line 1164). 3. **Composite index** — `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/stock_ledger_entry.py` line 366 adds the index `["item_code", "warehouse", "posting_datetime", "creation"]` precisely so these `(posting_datetime, creation)` sorts/compares are index‑backed. ## "Previous" selection for a given voucher — `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` (lines 1929–1970) This is the function that decides what "previous" means, and it has three modes: ```python def get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher(args, operator="<", exclude_current_voucher=False): ... elif args.get("creation") and args.get("sle_id") and not args.get("cancelled"): operator = "<=" voucher_condition = f"and creation < '{creation}'" ... order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update ``` - **Submit of a new voucher** (`repost_current_voucher` → `update_entries_after(sle_id=..., creation=..., cancelled=False)` → `initialize_previous_data`, lines 682, 172–199): the branch above fires, so "previous" = newest SLE with `posting_datetime <= mine` **and** `creation < my_creation`. Within a same‑second cluster, only entries created *earlier* can be your base — a sibling posted at the same second but submitted later is never counted as your "previous" (and your own voucher's rows are excluded because they share `creation`). - **Cancellation repost** (`cancelled=True`): the branch is skipped, the operator stays strictly `<`, so the anchor is the newest entry *strictly before* the posting second — no same‑second row is trusted as a base. - **Background repost** (`repost_stock_ledgers`, line 789): the anchor is fetched strictly before too, but that's safe because `get_future_entries_to_repost()` uses `posting_datetime >=` (line 903–904), so the *entire* same‑second cluster is pulled into the repost set and reprocessed in `creation` order anyway. ## The cancel scenario specifically (Purchase Receipt + Material Transfer at the same second) Flow in `make_sl_entries()` (lines 104–170): 1. `set_as_cancel()` (line 241) first flips **all** of the cancelling voucher's SLEs to `is_cancelled = 1`; the reversal SLE is also inserted with `is_cancelled = 1`. From here on, every ledger query filters `is_cancelled = 0`, so the cancelled transaction has vanished from the ledger. 2. `repost_current_voucher(..., cancelled=True)` → `update_entries_after` → `build()` → since `args.sle_id` is set, **`process_sle_against_current_timestamp()`** (line 938) runs, which calls **`get_sle_against_current_voucher()`** (lines 1906–1926): it selects *all non‑cancelled* SLEs at exactly that `posting_datetime` for the item/warehouse, `orderby creation asc`, `for update`. Note the key line: ```python if not kwargs.get("cancelled"): query = query.where(doctype.creation == kwargs.creation) ``` On submit it processes only the voucher's own rows; **on cancel the `creation` filter is dropped**, so the surviving same‑second voucher (the Material Transfer) is re‑processed in creation order from the clean strictly‑before anchor. `process_sle()` recomputes its `qty_after_transaction`, valuation rate, stock value/queue and `db_update()`s the row (lines 1130–1164) — i.e., the survivor's "current" balance is rebuilt as if the cancelled receipt never existed, using the agreed `(posting_datetime, creation)` ordering rather than whatever ambiguous order the original same‑second insert happened to produce. 3. `update_qty_in_future_sle()` (lines 2212–2265) then shifts later running balances. Its "future" definition is the same pair test: ```python future_condition = sle.posting_datetime > posting_datetime if args.get("creation") and not args.get("is_cancelled"): future_condition |= (sle.posting_datetime == posting_datetime) & (sle.creation > args["creation"]) ``` On cancel, only rows *strictly after* the second are bulk‑shifted — same‑second rows were already recomputed correctly in step 2. On submit, a same‑second but later‑created entry **is** shifted (documented by `test_update_qty_in_future_sle_shifts_same_timestamp_later_entry`, `test_stock_ledger_entry.py:1308`). 4. Boundary helpers use the identical pair semantics: `get_next_reco_datetime_condition()` (2304–2306), `get_datetime_limit_condition()` (2350–2352), `get_stock_value_difference()` (2603–2607), and `get_next_stock_reco()` orders by `posting_datetime` then `creation` (2336–2337). `test_get_next_stock_reco_respects_creation_order` (test file line 1367) and `test_backdated_sle_with_same_timestamp` (line 1267) pin this behavior. ## Why negative‑stock validation isn't fooled - **During reposting**, `update_entries_after.validate_negative_stock()` (line 1352) checks `qty_after_transaction + actual_qty − reserved_stock` against the running balance built from the correctly ordered chain (per item+warehouse), collecting into `self.exceptions` and raising `NegativeStockError` via `raise_exceptions()` (line 1833). Because the chain was re‑anchored and the same‑second cluster re‑run in `creation` order after the cancel, the survivor's balance is real, not a stale artifact of ambiguous ordering. - **Fast‑path check** `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle()` → `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty()` (lines 2355–2441) scans `is_cancelled = 0` rows with `posting_datetime >=` the event's datetime (so same‑second survivors are included), ordered by `(posting_datetime, creation)` — a surviving negative balance is detected no matter which of the same‑second rows would sort "first". - **Concurrency hardening**: `make_sl_entries` takes `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)` in sorted pair order (lines 117–120, 292–301) so two same‑second vouchers can't interleave writes or take locks in opposite order; the previous/future SLE selects use `for update`; background reposts serialize per (item, warehouse) via `repost_gate()`. - **Creation preservation**: when a cancelled Stock Reconciliation is re‑posted, `make_entry()` restores the original `creation` (`creation_time`, lines 263–264) so the recreated SLE keeps its original position in the `(posting_datetime, creation)` order. **Key functions:** `make_sl_entries`, `repost_current_voucher`, `update_entries_after` (`__init__`, `build`, `initialize_previous_data`, `sort_sles`, `repost_stock_ledgers`, `process_sle`, `process_sle_against_current_timestamp`, `validate_negative_stock`, `raise_exceptions`), `get_sle_against_current_voucher`, `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`, `get_stock_ledger_entries`, `update_qty_in_future_sle`, `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`, `get_next_stock_reco`/`get_datetime_limit_condition`, `set_as_cancel` — all in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`; plus `future_sle_exists` in `erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py` and the SLE composite indexes in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/stock_ledger_entry.py`.

## Short answer ERPNext never relies on `posting_datetime` alone. Every stock‑ledger read used for reposting and negative‑stock validation orders rows by the composite key **`(posting_datetime, creation)`**, where `creation` is the row's insertion timestamp (microsecond precision, strictly increasing with the order transactions actually hit the DB). Ties at the same second are therefore broken deterministically by insert order, and cancellation works by *removing* the cancelled rows from that ordering (`is_cancelled = 0`) and *replaying the entire surviving same‑second cohort* in creation order, rather than trusting stale `qty_after_transaction` values. ## The mechanics **1. The ordering key lives in the queries** — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`: - `get_stock_ledger_entries()` (L1994‑2081) — the workhorse: `where is_cancelled = 0 … order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}`. It backs `get_previous_sle()` (L1973, `<= desc limit 1`) and `get_future_entries_to_repost()` (L903, `>= asc … for update`). - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` (L1929‑1970) — the "previous SLE" selector, `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update`, always `is_cancelled = 0`. Crucially, when it's anchoring a specific live voucher SLE (`args` has `sle_id` + `creation` and `cancelled` is falsy), it forces `operator = "<="` **and** adds `creation < args.creation` (L1943‑1946). So on submission, among entries sharing the same posting second, only those *created before* the current SLE are treated as "previous" — a Purchase Receipt created earlier in wall‑clock time is correctly seen as previous to a Material Transfer posted at the same second, and not vice versa. - `get_sle_against_current_voucher()` (L1906‑1926) — selects live SLEs with `posting_datetime ==` the current second, `orderby(creation, asc).for_update()`. On **submit** it additionally filters `creation == kwargs.creation`, scoping the replay to the current voucher's own rows; on **cancel that filter is dropped** (`if not kwargs.get("cancelled")`, L1923‑1924). **2. What actually happens on cancellation** (e.g. cancelling the Material Transfer that shares second X with a Purchase Receipt): - The voucher's `get_sl_entries()` builds reversal dicts with `is_cancelled: 1` and the *original* posting date/time (`erpnext/stock/services/stock_ledger_service.py:86‑87,99`). `make_sl_entries()` (stock_ledger.py L104) then: 1. calls `set_as_cancel()` (L241) to flip **all** original SLEs of the voucher to `is_cancelled = 1` — they instantly vanish from every ordering query; 2. inserts reversal SLEs (also `is_cancelled = 1`, negated `actual_qty`, rates back‑filled via `get_incoming_outgoing_rate_for_cancel`) — these exist for GL/valuation and are excluded from all live‑state reads; 3. calls `repost_current_voucher(args, cancelled=True)` → `update_entries_after({sle_id: reversal.name, creation: reversal.creation, cancelled: True})`. - In `update_entries_after.build()` (L709), the `sle_id` path runs `process_sle_against_current_timestamp()` (L938) → `get_sle_against_current_voucher`. Because `cancelled=True`, the creation‑equality filter is off, so it fetches **every surviving SLE at exactly second X** (the PR's entries) in `creation` ASC order and reprocesses each through `process_sle()` (L993). The running balance is re‑anchored with `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` at default operator `<` (strictly *before* the second — the same‑second entries are part of the replay itself), and each processed entry becomes the new anchor via `self.prev_sle_dict[key] = sle` (L1164), physically rewriting `qty_after_transaction`/`stock_queue`/valuation (`db_update`, L1162). - `validate_negative_stock()` (L1352, "will not consider cancelled entries") runs per replayed SLE against this freshly derived balance minus `reserved_stock`; deficits are collected per warehouse and raised as `NegativeStockError` by `raise_exceptions()` (L1833). Since every query involved filters `is_cancelled = 0`, the cancelled transfer can't masquerade as either the "current" or the "previous" entry. **3. Future propagation keeps the same rule:** - `update_qty_in_future_sle()` (L2212‑2263): "future" = `posting_datetime > X`, plus — only for a *non‑cancelled* current entry — `(posting_datetime == X) & (creation > args.creation)`. On cancel the equality clause is skipped: same‑second survivors were already recomputed by the replay; only strictly later entries get the bulk `±qty_shift`. (Pinned by `test_update_qty_in_future_sle_shifts_same_timestamp_later_entry` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:1308`.) - `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle()` (L2355) → `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty()` (L2419): scans live entries with `posting_datetime >= X` — deliberately *inclusive* of the same second — `voucher_no !=` the cancelled voucher, `is_cancelled = 0`, `qty_after_transaction < 0`, `orderby(posting_datetime, creation)`, so the earliest genuine deficit in creation order is what throws, with correct voucher attribution. The batch variant sums `actual_qty over (order by posting_datetime, creation)` (L2444). - Same pattern in the boundary helpers: `get_next_reco_datetime_condition()` (L2298: `> X`, or `== X & creation > args.creation`, or `>= X` when cancelled), `get_datetime_limit_condition()` (L2347), `get_next_stock_reco()` (L2309), `sort_sles()` (L803 — the background `Repost Item Valuation` deque is sorted by `(posting_datetime, creation)`), and `future_sle_exists()` in `erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py:705` (`posting_datetime >= X`, `voucher_no !=`, `is_cancelled = 0`). **4. Concurrency guards** so the creation ordering can't be corrupted by parallel writes: `sle_processing_gate()` (L292, per‑(item, warehouse) advisory lock taken before any stock write) and `repost_gate()` (L276) serialize reposts, plus `for update` row locks on every previous/future read. ## Walkthrough of your example PR (+5) and MT (−3) both at second X, creations C1 < C2. Cancel the MT: 1. `set_as_cancel` flags MT's SLEs `is_cancelled=1`; reversal SLEs (also `is_cancelled=1`, posting X, creation C3 = now) are inserted. 2. `update_entries_after(cancelled=True)` re‑anchors on the latest live SLE with `posting_datetime < X`, then replays the surviving same‑second cohort — the PR's SLEs — in creation order, re‑deriving and rewriting their balances, and re‑running `validate_negative_stock` on each. 3. `update_qty_in_future_sle` shifts only strictly‑later entries by +3; `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` then scans live rows from X onward (inclusive, creation tie‑broken, MT excluded) — so a later Delivery Note that consumed the MT's stock is caught as genuinely negative, while the ambiguity of "who was first at second X" is settled purely by `creation`, never by voucher type or query luck. This behavior is pinned by tests `test_backdated_sle_with_same_timestamp` and `test_get_next_stock_reco_respects_creation_order` (same test file), and `test_set_as_cancel_marks_entries_cancelled` (`erpnext/stock/tests/test_stock_ledger.py:12`).

I now have the complete picture. Here's the full mechanism: ## The core problem: `posting_datetime` is only second-granular Every SLE stores `posting_datetime = get_combine_datetime(posting_date, posting_time)` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py:665`), so a Purchase Receipt (+10) and a Material Transfer (−4) submitted in the same second are indistinguishable by timestamp alone. ERPNext resolves this with a two-level key: **`posting_datetime` first, `creation` (the SLE row's insertion timestamp) second** — and `creation` is the deterministic, immutable tie-breaker. ## The ordering/selection machinery — all in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` | Function | Lines | Ordering / selection rule | |---|---|---| | `get_stock_ledger_entries` | 1994–2081 | `order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}`, always `is_cancelled = 0` | | `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` | 1929–1970 | `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1`, `is_cancelled = 0` | | `get_sle_against_current_voucher` | 1906–1926 | same-second bucket, `order by creation asc`, `for update` | | `sort_sles` (repost queue) | 803–810 | in-memory sort by `(posting_datetime, creation)` | ## What happens on cancellation 1. **`make_sl_entries` (L104)**: `cancelled = sl_entries[0].get("is_cancelled")` → `validate_cancellation` (L213, blocks/skips an in-flight `Repost Item Valuation`) → **`set_as_cancel` (L241)** marks *all* the voucher's SLEs `is_cancelled = 1` in place (rows are never deleted). The qty is negated and rates re-derived via `get_incoming_outgoing_rate_for_cancel`, then `repost_current_voucher(..., cancelled=cancelled)` (L172) calls `update_entries_after({... "sle_id": name, "creation": creation, "cancelled": cancelled})` (L572). 2. **Seeding "previous" — `initialize_previous_data` (L656) → `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher(self.args)`**, with this pivotal tie-break at L1943–1946: ```python elif args.get("creation") and args.get("sle_id") and not args.get("cancelled"): operator = "<=" voucher_condition = f"and creation < '{creation}'" ``` - **Normal (non-cancel) repost**: previous = latest non-cancelled SLE with `posting_datetime <= mine` **and `creation <` mine**. A same-second PR created earlier *does* count as previous — the tie is resolved by creation, never ambiguous. The voucher's *own* same-`creation` rows are excluded here on purpose. - **Cancellation repost** (`cancelled=1`): the `elif` is skipped, so the operator stays `<` — previous is the latest non-cancelled SLE **strictly before** that second. *No* same-second entry is trusted as the opening balance. 3. **Replaying the same-second bucket — `build()` (L709, `sle_id` branch) → `process_sle_against_current_timestamp` (L938) → `get_sle_against_current_voucher`**: it selects **every non-cancelled SLE at that exact `posting_datetime`** with `for update`. When `cancelled` is falsy it restricts to `creation == kwargs.creation` (only the current voucher's rows); when `cancelled=True` the filter is dropped — **all survivors from all vouchers are reprocessed in `creation asc` order**, chained over one shared running balance in `self.prev_sle_dict[(item_code, warehouse)]` via `process_sle` (L993). 4. **Negative-stock validation against the chained balance — `validate_negative_stock` (L1352)**: `diff = qty_after_transaction + actual_qty − reserved_stock`; failures are collected in `self.exceptions[warehouse]` (the loop continues to keep the chain consistent) and finally thrown by `raise_exceptions()` (L1833) as `NegativeStockError` ("X units of Y needed in Z on {date} {time} for {voucher}…"). Because the bucket is replayed sequentially in creation order, each SLE is validated against exactly the balance its same-second predecessor left — there is no "which equal-timestamp entry is current?" ambiguity to fool it. ## Worked example (PR +10 and MT −4 at the same second) - **Cancel the MT**: its rows become invisible (`is_cancelled=0` filter everywhere); previous = balance strictly before the second; the same-second bucket replays only the surviving PR; final balance and Bin (`update_bin`, L715) revert to the PR-only state. No false negative. - **Cancel the PR instead**: previous = strictly before the second; the surviving MT (−4) is replayed against that pre-receipt balance — if `diff < 0`, `raise_exceptions` throws `NegativeStockError` naming the MT voucher. Correctly *not* fooled into thinking the receipt is still there. ## Future-side guard (same transaction) After the current-voucher repost, `update_qty_in_future_sle` (L2212) shifts `qty_after_transaction` for future rows where `posting_datetime > dt` **OR** (`posting_datetime == dt` **and `creation >` mine**) — the same creation-based boundary; for a cancelled voucher only strictly-later timestamps are shifted (L2226–2229), since same-second survivors were fully recomputed in step 3. Then `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` (L2355) → `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty` (L2419) picks the first non-cancelled SLE with `posting_datetime >=` and `qty_after_transaction < 0`, ordered by `posting_datetime, creation`, and throws `NegativeStockError`. Backgound reposts (`repost_future_sle` L304 → `update_entries_after` without `sle_id` → `get_future_entries_to_repost` L903, `>=` query) re-sort the queue with `sort_sles`, preserving the same `(datetime, creation)` discipline. ## Extra hardening in this codebase - `sle_processing_gate` (L292) and `repost_gate` (L276): Postgres advisory locks serializing *all* stock writes per (item, warehouse), so two concurrent same-second writers can't both read the same stale "previous" SLE; `make_sl_entries` acquires the gates in sorted pair order (L119) to avoid deadlock. - `make_entry` (L252) preserves `creation` for re-posted Stock Reconciliations via `creation_time` (L263), and a re-submitted voucher naturally gets a *new, later* `creation`, deterministically sorting it after the other same-second voucher. **In short**: cancellation first makes the cancelled rows invisible (`is_cancelled = 1` filtered out of every query), then deliberately drops the same-second tie-break for the "previous" seed (strict `<`), and instead replays the entire surviving same-second bucket in `creation asc` order over a single chained balance — so negative-stock validation always sees the true sequential balance of surviving transactions, never an arbitrarily chosen "current/previous" pair from an ambiguous timestamp tie.

final answer
## Short answer ERPNext never orders the Stock Ledger by `posting_datetime` alone. Every ledger read/repost query sorts by the composite key **`(posting_datetime, creation)`**, where `creation` is the row's microsecond-precision insert timestamp. That gives a deterministic total order even when a Purchase Receipt and a Material Transfer share the exact same second. On cancellation, the reposting engine deliberately (a) starts its "previous" state **strictly before** the shared timestamp and (b) re-replays **all surviving same-timestamp entries** in `creation` order — so negative-stock validation runs against the true chronological running balance, not an ambiguous one. All of this lives in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. ## The canonical ordering rule - `get_stock_ledger_entries()` (`stock_ledger.py:1994-2081`) — the base query used by `get_previous_sle` (`<=, desc`), `get_sle_before_datetime` (`<, desc`), `get_sle_after_datetime` (`>, asc`) and `update_entries_after.get_future_entries_to_repost` (`>=, asc`, line 903) — always ends with: ```sql where is_cancelled = 0 ... and posting_datetime {op} %(posting_datetime)s order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order} ``` - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` (`:1929-1968`) — `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update`. - `get_sle_against_current_voucher()` (`:1906-1926`) — same-timestamp rows fetched `orderby(creation, asc)`. - Background reposting (`Repost Item Valuation` path): `update_entries_after.sort_sles()` (`:803-810`) sorts by `key=(posting_datetime, creation)`. - Negative-qty scans: `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty` (`:2419`) and the batch window `sum(actual_qty) over (order by posting_datetime, creation)` (`:2450`), plus `get_future_stock_vouchers` in `erpnext/accounts/utils.py:1772-1812` (`orderby(Min(posting_datetime)).orderby(Min(creation))`). `posting_datetime` itself is a denormalized column set in `make_sl_entries` via `get_combine_datetime(posting_date, posting_time)` (`:152`, `erpnext/stock/utils.py:665`). ## "Current" vs "previous" during reposting **On submission** (`cancelled=False`): `make_sl_entries` → `repost_current_voucher` (`:172`) → `update_entries_after` (`:572`) carries `sle_id` + `creation` of the new row. `initialize_previous_data` (`:656`) calls `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`, which hits the branch at `:1943-1946`: ```python elif args.get("creation") and args.get("sle_id") and not args.get("cancelled"): operator = "<=" voucher_condition = f"and creation < '{creation}'" ``` So "previous" = the latest non-cancelled entry with `posting_datetime <= current` **and creation < current's creation** — among same-second rows, only ones inserted earlier qualify. `get_sle_against_current_voucher` then processes only rows with `creation == kwargs.creation` (`:1923-1924`), i.e. the current voucher's own rows. **On cancellation** (`cancelled=True`): `set_as_cancel` (`:241`) flips `is_cancelled=1` on the voucher's rows (every query filters `is_cancelled = 0`, so they vanish); then `repost_current_voucher(..., cancelled=True)` runs. The creation-guard branch is **skipped** (`not args.get("cancelled")` fails), so the default strict operator `<` applies — the "previous" state is the last entry **strictly before** the shared timestamp. Same-timestamp rows are excluded from "previous" on purpose, because `build()` → `process_sle_against_current_timestamp()` (`:938`) → `get_sle_against_current_voucher` now drops the `creation ==` filter (`:1923-1924`) and returns **all surviving non-cancelled SLEs at that exact posting_datetime** — i.e. the un-cancelled Purchase Receipt (and anything else in that second) — in `creation asc` order. Each is replayed through `process_sle` (`:993`), whose running state `self.wh_data` is seeded from the strict-`<` previous SLE and chained via `self.prev_sle_dict[key] = sle` (`:1164`). Concretely, with PR(+10) and MT-out(−10) at 10:00:00 (PR inserted first, so its `creation` is smaller): - **Cancel the PR**: its rows are excluded; replay starts from the balance *before* 10:00:00 and re-applies the MT at its creation-based position, so the MT's `qty_after_transaction` is recomputed from the correct base rather than inheriting the cancelled PR's contribution. - **Cancel the MT**: its rows are excluded; the replay re-applies only the surviving PR. ## Why negative-stock validation isn't fooled 1. **Per-row during replay** — `process_sle` (`:1022-1027`) calls `validate_negative_stock` (`:1352-1370`): `diff = self.wh_data.qty_after_transaction + flt(sle.actual_qty) - flt(self.reserved_stock)`, against the running balance of the deterministic `(posting_datetime, creation)` sequence. Cancel the PR in the PR/MT example and the replayed MT-out yields `0 − 10 = −10` → a `NegativeStockError` exception (`raise_exceptions`, `:1833`) blocks the cancellation. The system can never "borrow" the cancelled receipt by ordering ambiguity, because the cancelled rows are already invisible and the survivor sits exactly where its `creation` puts it. 2. **Future rows after the repost** — `update_qty_in_future_sle` (`:2212-2263`) shifts `qty_after_transaction` with `posting_datetime > dt OR (posting_datetime == dt AND creation > args.creation)` (the second clause only when not cancelled — same-second survivors were already recomputed by the replay). It then calls `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` (`:2355`), which scans future rows via `posting_datetime >= args.posting_datetime`, `voucher_no != current`, ordered `(posting_datetime, creation)`, with precision tolerance in `is_negative_with_precision` (`:2403`). 3. Concurrency is handled too: the previous-SLE read is `for update` plus the per-`(item, warehouse)` `sle_processing_gate` (`:292`), so no concurrent insert can distort the `creation` ordering between the "previous" read and the write. The generic `get_previous_sle` (`:1973-1991`) used by voucher validations (`set_actual_qty`, `get_qty_after_transaction`, `has_correct_data`) also resolves same-timestamp ties by `creation desc` and excludes only the exact row via `name != %(name)s` (`:2055-2056`), but the reposting engine uses the purpose-built `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` with the `creation <` guard precisely to control the current/previous boundary. ## Regression tests pinning this behavior `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py`: - `test_tie_breaking` (`:1132`) — two Stock Entries at identical date/time assert `[10, 11]` in `(posting_datetime, creation)` order; after `first.cancel()` + `repost_entries()`, the survivor recomputes to `[1]`. - `test_timestamp_clash` (`:1192`) — consumption at `02:00:00.1234` vs a backdated receipt at `02:00:00` (ms stripped into the same bucket); cancelling the backdated receipt must not double-process qty. - `test_previous_sle_with_clashed_timestamp` (`:1227`), `test_backdated_sle_with_same_timestamp` (`:1267`), and `test_update_qty_in_future_sle_shifts_same_timestamp_later_entry` (`:1308`) — the last one explicitly documents that "future" means strictly later in the `(posting_datetime, creation)` order, not merely a different `posting_datetime`.

final answer
## Short answer For a genuine intra‑company PR (one created from the source Delivery Note), the incoming rate is **the value fixed at the time the source Delivery Note was made** — specifically the stored `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate`. A fresh, receipt‑time valuation lookup exists only as a fallback branch for rows *not* linked to a Delivery Note Item — and that fallback is effectively unreachable because validation forces the DN link on internal transfers. ## How it works, step by step **1. Detection of the internal transfer** - `AccountsController.is_internal_transfer()` (`erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py:1286`) delegates to `InternalTransferService.is_internal_transfer()` (`erpnext/accounts/services/internal_transfer.py:17`) — true when `is_internal_supplier` is set and `represents_company == company`. - During `AccountsController.validate()` (`accounts_controller.py:241‑244`), `InternalTransferService.validate()` runs, and `validate_reference()` (lines 75–102) **requires** `inter_company_reference` (the source DN) and a `delivery_note_item` link on every row, throwing otherwise. Those links are populated by the mapper `make_inter_company_purchase_receipt()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/mapper.py:409`, field map `"name": "delivery_note_item"` at line 572). **2. The rate itself** `AccountsController.validate()` calls `self.set_incoming_rate()` → `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:606`), which for a non‑return internal transfer calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer()` (`buying_controller.py:647`). It has two branches: - **Linked row (the normal, mandatory case)** — `buying_controller.py:683‑687`: reads the stored field straight from the DB row of the source `Delivery Note Item`: `field = "incoming_rate" if self.get("is_internal_supplier") else "rate"`, multiplied by `conversion_factor`. This is the value **frozen when the DN was made**, stored into `Purchase Receipt Item.sales_incoming_rate`. - **Unlinked row (fallback)** — `buying_controller.py:664‑681`: computes the outgoing rate **fresh at PR posting time** via `erpnext.stock.utils.get_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py:244`, FIFO/Moving‑Average/batch/serial against `from_warehouse` and the PR's posting datetime). As noted, `validate_reference()` blocks this case for valid internal transfers. **3. Where that "fixed" value came from** — On the Delivery Note, `SellingController.set_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py:515`, branch at 578–617) computes `d.incoming_rate = get_incoming_rate(...)` against the DN's own source warehouse **at DN posting time** (the item's valuation rate then), and for internal transfers forces `d.rate = incoming_rate × conversion_factor` (lines 649–663) unless arms‑length pricing is allowed. **4. Rate enforcement / arms‑length option** — Back in `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate()` (lines 625–645): if Stock Settings `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is off (default), the PR item's `rate` is overwritten with `sales_incoming_rate` and discounts/margins zeroed ("Item rate has been updated as per valuation rate…"). If on, the entered commercial price is kept, but valuation still uses `sales_incoming_rate`. (Verified by `test_16_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price`, `erpnext/controllers/tests/test_accounts_controller.py:720‑779`.) **5. Into valuation and the ledger** — `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate()` (`buying_controller.py:414`, called from `validate()` at line 69) uses `net_rate = item.qty * item.sales_incoming_rate` (lines 465‑466, 529‑530) to compute `item.valuation_rate` (plus item tax and landed costs); `update_stock_ledger()` then posts the receiving‑warehouse SLE with `"incoming_rate": d.valuation_rate` (`buying_controller.py:833`). **6. Ledger‑level anchoring (safety net)** — When SLEs are processed or reposted, `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` detects internal‑transfer PR/PI rows (`is_internal_transfer(sle)`, line 1035 and 1470) and **overrides** the rate with `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer(sle)` (line 2540), which re‑fetches the linked `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` plus any per‑row landed‑cost amount — again the DN‑time value, not a fresh valuation. The test `test_internal_transfer_pr_incoming_sle_anchored_to_dn_rate` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/test_purchase_receipt.py:1912`) documents exactly this: even if `PR Item.valuation_rate`/`sales_incoming_rate` are tampered with, the inward SLE stays anchored to the DN's rate so no "divisional loss" leaks into COGS. **7. Repost behavior** — `RepostItemValuation._recalculate_valuation_rate()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py:369‑376`) re-runs `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer()` for docs with `is_internal_supplier`, so after a back‑dated repost the PR re-reads the (possibly updated) DN item value rather than revaluing at its own posting time. ## Conclusion The system deliberately propagates the cost fixed at the source Delivery Note (`Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate`, itself the source warehouse's valuation rate at DN time) through `sales_incoming_rate` → `valuation_rate` → the inward SLE, and even hard‑anchors the SLE to that value at ledger level. Fresh recomputation at receipt time (`get_incoming_rate` in `buying_controller.py:664‑681`) exists only as a fallback for unlinked rows, which the mandatory DN‑reference validation prevents in the standard internal‑transfer flow.

final answer
## Summary For an intra‑company (internal) transfer, the Purchase Receipt's incoming rate is **the value fixed at the source Delivery Note** — the `incoming_rate` stored on the linked `Delivery Note Item` row (i.e., the source warehouse's valuation at DN posting time). A fresh computation at receipt time happens only as a fallback when the item row has no DN link, which is normally prevented by validation. ## The mechanism, step by step **1. DN side — the rate is frozen at Delivery Note time.** `SellingController.set_incoming_rate` (`erpnext/controllers/selling_controller.py:515`) computes `d.incoming_rate` via `get_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/stock/utils.py`) against the *source* warehouse at the DN's posting date/time — and it forces this computation whenever `self.is_internal_transfer()` (line 592). That value is persisted on the `Delivery Note Item` row and its SLE. **2. PR creation — the link is established.** `make_inter_company_purchase_receipt` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/mapper.py:409`) → `make_inter_company_transaction` sets `is_internal_supplier = 1` and `inter_company_reference` (lines 465–471), and `set_purchase_references` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/sales_invoice/mapper.py:408`) back-links each `Purchase Receipt Item` to its source row via the `delivery_note_item` field. **3. PR validate — the DN rate is pulled in.** `AccountsController.validate` (`erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py:244`) calls `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:606`), gated by `InternalTransferService.is_internal_transfer` (`erpnext/accounts/services/internal_transfer.py:17` — true when `is_internal_supplier` and `represents_company == company`). It then calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer` (line 647), which for each item: - **With a `delivery_note_item` link** (the normal case): reads the **stored** `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` — `field = "incoming_rate" if self.get("is_internal_supplier") else "rate"` (line 683) — into `d.sales_incoming_rate` (× conversion factor). Since `InternalTransferService.validate_reference` (lines 75–102) *throws* if any internal-transfer PR item lacks `delivery_note_item`, the "fixed at DN" path is effectively mandatory. - **Without a link** (fallback): recomputes fresh via `get_incoming_rate()` against `from_warehouse` at the PR's posting time (lines 664–681). Unless `Stock Settings > allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is enabled, it then forces `d.rate = d.sales_incoming_rate` (zeroing discounts/margins) with the alert "Item rate has been updated as per valuation rate since its an internal stock transfer." **4. Valuation.** `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate` (line 414) deliberately ignores the PR's own net amount for internal transfers: `if item.sales_incoming_rate: net_rate = item.qty * item.sales_incoming_rate` (lines 465–466, also 529–530 for item tax), so `valuation_rate = (sales_incoming_rate × qty + item_tax_amount + landed_cost_voucher_amount) / stock_qty`. **5. SLE — anchored even on reposting.** `BuyingController.update_stock_ledger` (line 831–838) puts `incoming_rate = d.valuation_rate` with `recalculate_rate = 1` on the receiving-warehouse SLE. During SLE processing and any later reposting, `update_entries_after.get_dynamic_incoming_outgoing_rate` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1372`) → `get_incoming_outgoing_rate_from_transaction` (line 1467–1472) → `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer` (line 2540), which re-reads `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` through the PR item's `delivery_note_item` link (plus `landed_cost_voucher_amount / abs(actual_qty)`). So even when the ledger is rebuilt (stock reconciliation, LCV, backdated reposts), the inward SLE is re-anchored to the DN's rate, not recomputed from the receiving warehouse's current stock value. The test `test_internal_transfer_pr_incoming_sle_anchored_to_dn_rate` (`test_purchase_receipt.py:1912–1996`) proves exactly this: even with `PR item.valuation_rate` and the SLE's `incoming_rate` corrupted to 80, `update_entries_after` restores them to the DN's 100 so no divisional profit/loss leaks into COGS. ## Caveat: arms-length pricing With `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` enabled, `set_incoming_rate` skips overriding `d.rate`, so the PR may carry an arms-length transaction price — but stock *valuation* still uses the DN-derived rate: in `test_16_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` (`erpnext/controllers/tests/test_accounts_controller.py:720–779`), the item rate stays at 40 while `valuation_rate` remains 100 (the DN rate). (The reposter also re-runs this sync: `RepostItemValuation._recalculate_valuation_rate` calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer` before `update_valuation_rate` — `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py:369–376`.) **Bottom line:** the incoming rate is the value fixed on the source Delivery Note (`Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate`), propagated via the `delivery_note_item` link into `sales_incoming_rate` → item rate/`valuation_rate` → inward SLE, and re-enforced on every repost; a fresh at-receipt-time computation is only the no-link fallback.

I now have the complete picture, verified across the controller, service, ledger, and test code. Here is the full answer. ## Short answer The Purchase Receipt's item cost for an intra-company transfer is **anchored to the rate recorded on the source Delivery Note** — specifically the stored `incoming_rate` on the linked `Delivery Note Item` row, fixed when the DN was posted (its outbound valuation). It is **not** recomputed independently at receipt time. A fresh receipt-time computation exists only as a fallback when the item row has no DN reference (which validation normally makes impossible). ## The mechanism, step by step **1. PR creation (mapper)** — `make_inter_company_purchase_receipt()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/mapper.py` (L409) maps each `Delivery Note Item` row into a `Purchase Receipt Item` and records the link via `"name": "delivery_note_item"` (L570-577). It sets `is_internal_supplier = 1` and `inter_company_reference` (L466-471). Note the item's `rate` is *not* force-mapped; rate logic happens at validation. **2. Validation — rate is pulled from the DN row** — `AccountsController.validate()` calls `self.set_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py` L244), which lands in `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate()` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py` L606-645). For a non-return internal transfer (per `InternalTransferService.is_internal_transfer()`, `erpnext/accounts/services/internal_transfer.py` L15-27: internal supplier + `represents_company == company`), it calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer()` (L647-687): - **If the row has a `delivery_note_item` reference** (the normal case — `InternalTransferService.validate_reference()` at L75-102 makes this field *mandatory* for internal-transfer PRs): `d.sales_incoming_rate = DN Item.incoming_rate × conversion_factor`. The field chosen is `"incoming_rate"` when `is_internal_supplier` is set — i.e., the valuation rate at which the DN's outbound SLE consumed the stock, frozen on the DN row at DN time. - **Only if there is no reference row** does it compute a fresh rate via `get_incoming_rate({...from_warehouse, PR posting_date/time...})` against the source warehouse ledger (L664-681) — the receipt-time fallback. Unless `Stock Settings.allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is enabled (L625-629), the PR item's `rate` is then overwritten with `sales_incoming_rate` (discounts and margins zeroed, L631-645). **3. Valuation basis** — `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate()` uses the anchored value as the cost basis instead of the billed net amount: `net_rate = item.qty * item.sales_incoming_rate` (L465-466, and the same in `get_item_tax_amount()` L529-530). So `valuation_rate = sales_incoming_rate-based net + valuation taxes + landed costs`, divided by stock-UOM qty (L481-486). The `sales_incoming_rate` field itself is persisted on `Purchase Receipt Item` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt_item/purchase_receipt_item.json` L1098) and is explicitly excluded from rounding (`erpnext/controllers/taxes_and_totals.py` L228). **4. Stock Ledger Entries — hard anchor at posting time** — even beyond the item fields, when the ledger processes a PR/PI SLE for an internal transfer, `process_sle()` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` (L1032-1044) calls `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer(sle)` (L2540-2568), which re-reads `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` for the linked row (plus any prorated `landed_cost_voucher_amount`) and forces `sle.incoming_rate` (inward leg) or `sle.outgoing_rate` (outbound leg) to it. The code comment is explicit: *"Anchor both legs of an internal-transfer PR/PI to the DN/SI incoming_rate; otherwise an inward SLE that inherits a stale PR.valuation_rate leaks the gap to COGS via divisional_loss."* **5. On backdated reposts** — `RepostItemValuation._recalculate_valuation_rate()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py` L369-376) re-invokes `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer()` before `update_valuation_rate()`, so the PR keeps mirroring the DN's current ledger-derived `incoming_rate` rather than re-valuing on its own. ## Evidence in tests - `test_internal_transfer_pr_incoming_sle_anchored_to_dn_rate` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/test_purchase_receipt.py` L1912-1996): even after deliberately corrupting `PR Item.valuation_rate`/SLE `incoming_rate` to 80, a repost restores both to 100 = the DN's `incoming_rate`. - The earlier internal-transfer test (L1855-1898) shows the flip side: after a backdated receipt revalues the source, `pr1.items[0].valuation_rate` follows the DN's revalued cost (200) while the transaction `rate` stays at the originally agreed 100. ## Summary of the division of labor | Concern | Where | Rate used | |---|---|---| | `is_internal_transfer` check | `InternalTransferService.is_internal_transfer()` (accounts/services/internal_transfer.py L15) | — | | Item `rate` / `sales_incoming_rate` | `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate` → `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer` (buying_controller.py L606/L647) | **Stored `DN Item.incoming_rate`** (fallback: fresh `get_incoming_rate` if unlinked) | | `valuation_rate` | `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate` (L465) | `sales_incoming_rate` + valuation taxes/landed costs | | SLE inward/outward rate | `process_sle` → `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer` (stock_ledger.py L1032/L2540) | **Stored `DN Item.incoming_rate`** + LCV amount | | Repost | `RepostItemValuation._recalculate_valuation_rate` (L369) | Re-reads the DN-anchored value | So: the value fixed on the source Delivery Note governs; the "fresh at receipt time" computation is only the degenerate fallback for rows lacking a DN reference.

final answer
I now have the complete picture, verified end-to-end. Here's the answer. ## Short answer For an intra-company transfer, the Purchase Receipt **anchors to the rate fixed at the time the source Delivery Note was posted** — specifically the `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` (the item's stock valuation in the issuing company's warehouse at DN time). It is *not* recomputed from the receiving warehouse's books at receipt time. A "fresh" valuation is computed only as a fallback when the PR row has no `delivery_note_item` link (which validation normally makes impossible). The anchoring is enforced at **two independent levels** — document validation and stock-ledger processing — so even a tampered/stale PR rate gets corrected. ## How it works, step by step **1. Creation — the link is established.** `make_inter_company_purchase_receipt` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/delivery_note/mapper.py:409`, via `make_inter_company_transaction:413`) maps the DN's `target_warehouse` → PR's `from_warehouse`, sets `is_internal_supplier = 1` and `inter_company_reference`, and crucially maps each `Delivery Note Item.name` → `Purchase Receipt Item.delivery_note_item` (mapper.py:572). `InternalTransferService.validate_reference` (`erpnext/accounts/services/internal_transfer.py:75-102`) throws "Internal Sales Reference Missing" if any row lacks this link, and `StockInternalTransferService.validate_internal_transfer` (`erpnext/stock/services/internal_transfer.py:24-61`) makes `from_warehouse` mandatory — so an internal-transfer PR is a two-legged SLE voucher (out of `from_warehouse`, into `warehouse`). **2. Document-level rate (`sales_incoming_rate`).** During validate, `AccountsController.validate` (`erpnext/controllers/accounts_controller.py:244`) calls `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate` (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:606-645`), which runs only for PR / update-stock PI, non-return, `is_internal_transfer()` (i.e. `is_internal_supplier` + `represents_company == company`, per `InternalTransferService.is_internal_transfer`, internal_transfer.py:17-27). It calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer` (`buying_controller.py:647-687`): - **With the `delivery_note_item` link (the normal, mandatory path):** `sales_incoming_rate = Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate × conversion_factor` — the **DN-time value** (line 683-687). - **Without the link (fallback):** it computes `get_incoming_rate(...)` (from `erpnext.stock.utils`, line 26) **fresh at the PR's posting date/time** against `from_warehouse` — the only "computed at receipt time" path, and even then it's the source-warehouse outgoing valuation, not the receiving side's. Unless Stock Settings → `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is set, it then forces `d.rate = d.sales_incoming_rate`, zeroing discounts/margins (lines 625-645, with the "Item rate has been updated as per valuation rate" alert). **3. PR valuation.** `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate` (`buying_controller.py:414-490`, called at `validate` line 68-69) uses `if item.sales_incoming_rate: net_rate = item.qty * item.sales_incoming_rate` (lines 464-466), so `valuation_rate` = DN-anchored net amount + `item_tax_amount` + `landed_cost_voucher_amount`, per stock-UOM qty — i.e., the DN value plus only charges added on the PR itself. **4. Ledger-level enforcement (the hard anchor).** `process_sle` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:993`, hook at lines 1032-1044): for any PR/PI SLE where `is_internal_transfer(sle)` (stock_ledger.py:2571-2580), both legs are re-anchored via `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer` (stock_ledger.py:2540-2567), which reads `Delivery Note Item.incoming_rate` through the row's `delivery_note_item` link and adds `landed_cost_voucher_amount / qty`. The outgoing leg gets `sle.outgoing_rate = rate`, the inward leg gets `sle.incoming_rate = rate`. The code comment explains why: otherwise "an inward SLE that inherits a stale PR.valuation_rate leaks the gap to COGS via divisional_loss." Additionally, `update_outgoing_rate_on_transaction` → `update_rate_on_purchase_receipt` (stock_ledger.py:1504-1522, 1574-1588) writes the recomputed rate back into the PR Item's `valuation_rate` in the DB. **5. Resilience to drift.** Because the ledger hook re-reads the DN on every SLE processing/repost (`update_entries_after`), even a PR whose stored `sales_incoming_rate`/`valuation_rate` got corrupted is re-valued from the DN. `test_purchase_receipt.py:1915+` simulates exactly this (sets `sales_incoming_rate: 0, valuation_rate: 80` via direct DB write) and asserts the inward SLE is re-anchored to the DN's `incoming_rate` (100). **The one exception — "arms length" pricing.** With `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` enabled, only the *commercial* `rate` on the PR may differ (no forced reset in step 2), but stock valuation stays DN-anchored: `test_accounts_controller.py:720-779` asserts `pi.items[0].rate == 40` (arms-length) while `valuation_rate == 100` (the internal transfer rate). So: the system deliberately preserves cost continuity across the internal supply chain — the receiving company's stock enters at exactly what it was worth when it left the selling company's warehouse (plus any landed costs/taxes added on the PR), fixed at DN time, and every repost re-derives it from the source DN rather than from receipt-time conditions.

I now have the complete picture, verified against the code and the regression tests. Here's the full answer. ## Context: what the Purchase Receipt already booked Assuming perpetual inventory (`Company.enable_perpetual_inventory`) and a Standard Cost item (say standard rate **130**, received at **200**), the PR (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`) posts: - **Debit Stock (inventory) account** = `stock_value_diff` from the SLE, which for a Standard Cost item is `qty × standard rate` (130) — `make_item_asset_inward_gl_entry` - **Credit "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB)** = the PR's `base_net_amount` (200) — `make_stock_received_but_not_billed_entry` - **Debit Purchase Price Variance (PPV) account** = the 70 difference — `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` → `get_divisional_loss_account`, which routes the difference to `get_purchase_price_variance_account()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:334`) for Standard Cost items (other items go to `default_expense_account`) ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock **OFF** **Account selection** — `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:20`): for a stock item with a linked PR, it checks that SRBNB was actually credited in that PR's GL entries and **forces `item.expense_account = stock_received_but_not_billed`**. **GL posting** — `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`, `else` branch, lines 319–350) posts a **single entry per item**: > **Debit: Stock Received But Not Billed — 200 (full billed `base_amount`), against the Supplier** The code comment spells out the design: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier — booking PPV again would double count it."* No Stock account, no PPV account, no Stock Ledger Entry. (Peripheral extras: exchange-rate-discrepancy entries if the invoice conversion rate differs from the PR's, lines 352–393; and an SRBNB debit + valuation-tax credit if the PR didn't book `item_tax_amount`, lines 395–439.) Result: SRBNB is fully cleared (200 debit wipes the 200 credit); the 70 variance **stays on the PPV account from the PR**. This is codified in `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/test_item_standard_cost.py:794`): asserts `booked(ppv_account) == 0` and `booked(srbnb_account) == 200`. ## Purchase Invoice with Update Stock **ON** **Account selection** — same `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account`, but with `update_stock` set and a warehouse present, `item.expense_account` becomes the **warehouse's Stock (inventory) account** (via `get_inventory_account_map`/`get_inventory_account_dict` in `erpnext/controllers/stock_controller.py`). **GL posting** — `make_item_gl_entries` now takes the stock branch (lines 180–269), and since the invoice itself does the receipt, the variance is booked **on the invoice**: 1. `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (lines 535–603) computes `warehouse_debit_amount = valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`, where `valuation_rate` is the invoice billed value per unit (`update_valuation_rate`, `erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:414` — net rate + item tax + landed cost). It compares this against the actual SLE `stock_value_difference` (which for Standard Cost items is `qty × standard rate` = 130). On mismatch it posts **Debit: PPV account** (`get_stock_variance_account`, lines 523–533) for the 70 difference, against the stock account, and reduces the stock debit to 130. 2. Then the main entry (lines 251–269): **Debit: warehouse Stock account — 130 (SLE stock value), against the Supplier** (plus landed-cost-voucher and sub-contracting entries when applicable). ## Summary of the difference | | Update Stock OFF (vs PR) | Update Stock ON | |---|---|---| | Debit 1 | SRBNB 200 | Warehouse Stock account 130 | | Debit 2 | — | PPV account 70 | | Supplier credit | 200 | 200 | | PPV booked where | Already on PR; invoice does **not** re-book | On the invoice itself | | Stock ledger | Untouched (PR did it) | New SLEs created by the invoice | Both paths net to the same supplier liability of 200; the difference is only whether the stock + variance legs are reused from the PR (invoice merely clears SRBNB) or freshly posted by the invoice.
