I have the full picture now. Here's the answer. ## Setup (as assumed by the code and its tests) Perpetual inventory is on for the company (`auto_accounting_for_stock`), the item is a stock item with **Valuation Method = "Standard Cost"**, and it was received on a Purchase Receipt. The repo's own test (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/test_item_standard_cost.py:794`, `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance`) uses: standard cost **130**, PR billed at **200**. The PR itself posts: **Dr Inventory 130 / Dr Purchase Price Variance (PPV) 70 / Cr Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB) 200** — the SLE is forced to the standard rate by `process_standard_cost` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:970-991`), and the billed-vs-standard gap goes to PPV via `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` → `get_divisional_loss_account` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py:233-273, 370-392`). ## Case 1 — Invoice with Update Stock **off** (against the PR) 1. **Expense head is rewritten to SRBNB.** `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:41-102`) sees `doc.update_stock` is falsy, finds the item in `doc.get_stock_items()`, checks whether the linked Purchase Receipt credited the company's "Stock Received But Not Billed" account, and (since it did) forces `item.expense_account = stock_not_billed_account`, with an "Expense Head Changed" msgprint if the row had a different account. 2. **One item GL entry: debit SRBNB at the full billed amount.** In `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`), the update-stock branch (lines 180-317) is skipped, so the row falls into the plain branch at lines 319-350, which debits `expense_account` (= SRBNB) with `base_net_amount` against the supplier. The comment there (lines 332-336) states the intent explicitly: the PR already booked the stock at standard and the Purchase Price Variance, so the invoice only clears SRBNB at the billed value — re-booking PPV would double-count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared. So the item-side entries are just: - **Dr Stock Received But Not Billed — 200** (vs. Cr Supplier, net total basis) - No inventory-account entry, no PPV entry. `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (line 535) is only called in the update-stock branch, so no variance is re-booked. The test asserts exactly this: `booked(ppv_account) == 0` and `booked(srbnb_account) == 200` for the invoice (lines 823-825). Together with the PR, SRBNB nets to zero, inventory carries 130 at standard, PPV carries 70. ## Case 2 — Invoice with Update Stock **enabled** Here the invoice itself is the receiving document, and its `make_item_gl_entries` takes the stock branch (lines 180-269): 1. **Expense account = the warehouse's inventory account** (`expense_account.py:51-54`). 2. **Variance routing.** `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (gl_composer.py:535-603) computes the document valuation `valuation_rate × qty` (valuation rate = billed net rate + valuation taxes + landed cost, per `BuyingController.update_valuation_rate`, `erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:481-486`) and compares it against the invoice's own SLE `stock_value_difference` — which is standard-valued (130) because the SLE valuation is forced to the standard rate. The difference is debited to `get_stock_variance_account(item)` (lines 523-533), which for a Standard Cost item returns the **Purchase Price Variance account** (`get_purchase_price_variance_account`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:334-353` — per-company Item Default override, else Company default); `warehouse_debit_amount` is then reset to the standard-valued SLE amount. 3. **Main entry:** **Dr Warehouse Inventory account** at the standard value (130) against the supplier. Net item side with Update Stock on: **Dr Inventory 130 + Dr PPV 70 = Cr Supplier 200** — i.e., the invoice reproduces the PR's own accounting, with SRBNB never touched. ## The difference in one line | | Update Stock off | Update Stock on | |---|---|---| | Expense account used | Stock Received But Not Billed (forced by `set_expense_account`) | Warehouse inventory account | | Inventory account debited | No (PR already did, at standard) | Yes, at the standard value | | Purchase Price Variance | **Not re-booked** (deliberately — comment at gl_composer.py:332-336; PR already booked it) | **Booked by the invoice** via `make_stock_adjustment_entry` for the billed-vs-standard gap | | Net effect | Clears the PR's SRBNB liability at the billed value (Dr SRBNB 200) | Books the receipt itself: Dr Inventory 130 / Dr PPV 70 / Cr Supplier 200 | Everything is wired through `PurchaseInvoice.get_gl_entries` → `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.compose` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:18-49`), and the no-rebook behavior is pinned by the regression test `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance`.

I have the full picture now, verified through the code and the standard-cost test suite. Here's the complete answer. ## Context: what the Purchase Receipt already posted Before the invoice exists, the submitted PR (with perpetual inventory enabled) posts, for each stock item row, in `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer._make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`): - **Dr** Warehouse/Stock asset account = `stock_value_difference` from the SLE (for a Standard Cost item, qty × standard rate, e.g. 130) - **Cr** "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB) = the row's `base_net_amount` (the receipt value, e.g. 200) - **Dr** Purchase Price Variance account = the gap (200 − 130 = 70), via `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` → `get_divisional_loss_account`, which for `get_valuation_method(...) == "Standard Cost"` returns `get_purchase_price_variance_account()` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:L334` — Item Default `purchase_price_variance_account`, else Company `default_purchase_price_variance_account`). ## Scenario A — PI against that PR with Update Stock OFF Expense-head resolution in `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py:L20`): since the item is a stock item and `update_stock` is off, it falls to the L56–82 branch — it checks whether the PR actually credited SRBNB (`frappe.db.exists("GL Entry", {voucher_type: "Purchase Receipt", voucher_no: item.purchase_receipt, account: stock_not_billed_account})`) and, if so, **forces `item.expense_account = "Stock Received But Not Billed"`** (with an "Expense Head Changed" msgprint on validate if it differed). `set_against_expense_account` then propagates that into `against_expense_account`. GL composition in `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`), item side = the `else` branch of `make_item_gl_entries` (L319–350): - **Dr "Stock Received But Not Billed" = item's full billed `base_net_amount`**, `against` the supplier. The rationale comment at L332–336 states this explicitly: the PR already booked the stock (at standard) and the PPV; re-booking the variance here would double-count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared. - The balancing **Cr Supplier (`credit_to`) = grand total** comes from `make_supplier_gl_entry` (L80–127), `against` = `against_expense_account` (SRBNB). - No inventory debit, no PPV entry, no Stock Ledger Entry (`update_stock_ledger` is only called when `update_stock == 1`, `purchase_invoice.py:L633`). - Only extra expense-side entry: if the PR was made at a different exchange rate, a discrepancy pair (Dr SRBNB / Cr `exchange_gain_loss_account`, L352–393). The test `test_pi_without_update_stock_does_not_rebook_variance` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/test_item_standard_cost.py:L794`) pins this down exactly: standard 130, PR @ 200 → PI books **PPV = 0, SRBNB debit = 200** (fully clearing the interim credit at the billed value). So the invoice's expense side is purely a **clearing entry**: Debit SRBNB / Credit Supplier. The capitalization (Dr Stock) and the variance (Dr PPV) were already recognized by the PR. ## Scenario B — PI with Update Stock enabled First, this combination is impossible against an existing PR: `validate_purchase_receipt_if_update_stock` (`purchase_invoice.py:L586–595`, called from `validate` L299) throws *"Stock cannot be updated for Purchase Invoice {0} because a Purchase Receipt {1} has already been created…"*. So an Update-Stock invoice is always the voucher that does the receipt itself. Then `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (L51–54) **overrides the expense head to the receiving warehouse's inventory account** (`get_inventory_account_map`), and the item side takes the stock branch of `make_item_gl_entries` (L180+): 1. `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (L535–603): computes `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor` (billed value) and compares it to the SLE's `stock_value_difference` (qty × standard rate for a Standard Cost item). On a mismatch it posts **Dr variance account** = difference, `against` the inventory account, and resets `warehouse_debit_amount` to the SLE value. The account comes from `get_stock_variance_account` (L523–533): **the Purchase Price Variance account for Standard Cost items**, company `default_expense_account` otherwise. 2. **Dr item.expense_account (= warehouse inventory/asset account) = actual SLE stock value**, `against` supplier (L252–269). 3. `update_stock_ledger()` runs before `make_gl_entries()` in `on_submit` (L633–639), followed by `repost_future_sle_and_gle()`; valuation-type taxes get their own SRBNB/tax-account entries (L395–439, L682–700). Net effect for the example (standard 130, billed 200): **Dr Inventory 130 + Dr Purchase Price Variance 70 / Cr Supplier 200** — the invoice itself capitalizes stock at standard and recognizes the PPV, plus a stock movement. ## The difference in one line | | Update Stock OFF (vs PR) | Update Stock ON | |---|---|---| | Expense-side debit | SRBNB only, at full billed value | Warehouse inventory account at SLE stock value | | PPV | None on the invoice (PR already booked it) | Booked on the invoice for billed-vs-standard gap | | Stock ledger | Untouched (blocked against PR anyway) | SLE created by the invoice | | Supplier credit | Grand total against `against_expense_account` | Same, but `against` the inventory account |

All verified. Here's the complete answer. ## The two-stage accounting design ERPNext splits a standard-cost purchase into two events: the **receipt** books inventory and the purchase-price variance (PPV); the **invoice** merely settles the liability. Both halves live in service classes: `ExpenseAccountService` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/expense_account.py`) decides which account the item's row debits, and `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py:129`) builds the entries. ### 1. Update Stock OFF, billed against the Purchase Receipt **Account resolution** — `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (expense_account.py:41-102): for a stock item under perpetual inventory, the row is *not* debited to a real expense account. Because `item.purchase_receipt` is set and the PR credited the company's `stock_received_but_not_billed` account, the service **overwrites `item.expense_account = "Stock Received But Not Billed"`** (line 82, with an "Expense Head Changed" msgprint if you had typed something else). **GL entries** — `make_item_gl_entries` skips its entire stock branch (`doc.update_stock` is falsy, so no `make_stock_adjustment_entry`, no inventory debit, and no Stock Ledger Entries at all) and falls into the `else` at line 319. For the item's expense side it posts exactly **one entry** (lines 337-350): - **Debit: Stock Received But Not Billed** = `base_net_amount` (the full billed amount), against the Supplier (which is credited via `make_supplier_gl_entry`, gl_composer.py:80-127). No PPV entry, no expense-account debit, no stock-account touch. The code's own comment (lines 332-336) states why: *"the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock (at standard) and the Purchase Price Variance. Here we only clear 'Stock Received But Not Billed' at the full billed amount against the supplier — booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partially uncleared."* **What the PR already booked** (so the invoice's single debit closes it): in `PurchaseReceiptGLComposer` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`) — Debit warehouse stock account with `stock_value_diff`, which for a Standard Cost item is qty × **standard cost**, because `stock_ledger.py:process_standard_cost` (lines 970-991) forces every inbound SLE's `incoming_rate` to the Item Standard Cost rate; Credit "Stock Received But Not Billed" with the PR's `base_net_amount` (lines 74-124); and the gap between document value and standard stock value goes through `make_divisional_loss_gl_entry` → `get_divisional_loss_account` (lines 370-384), which routes Standard Cost items to the **Purchase Price Variance account** (`get_purchase_price_variance_account`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:334` — Item Default override, else Company `default_purchase_price_variance_account`). Secondary entries in the same OFF case: an exchange-rate change between PR and invoice at the same net rate adds a Debit SRBNB + Credit `exchange_gain_loss_account` (gl_composer.py:352-393); valuation taxes (`item_tax_amount`) not booked in the PR add another Debit SRBNB and feed `negative_expense_to_be_booked` (lines 395-439). ### 2. Update Stock ON First, this combination is mutually exclusive with the PR flow: `validate_purchase_receipt_if_update_stock` (purchase_invoice.py:586-595) throws *"Stock cannot be updated… because a Purchase Receipt has already been created"* — so an Update-Stock invoice is a standalone receipt+bill. `set_expense_account` now sets `item.expense_account = warehouse inventory account` (expense_account.py:51-54), and `make_item_gl_entries` takes the stock branch (gl_composer.py:180-317): 1. **`make_stock_adjustment_entry`** (lines 535-603) computes `warehouse_debit_amount = valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor` (the billed rate) and compares it with the invoice's **own SLE** `stock_value_difference` — which is qty × **standard cost** (`process_standard_cost`). Any mismatch posts **Debit: Purchase Price Variance account** (via `get_stock_variance_account`, lines 523-533) for `billed − standard`, remarks "Stock Adjustment", against the inventory account, then resets `warehouse_debit_amount` to the SLE value. *This is where the PPV is booked when the invoice does its own receipt.* 2. **Debit: warehouse inventory account** (`item.expense_account`) with that standard-valued `warehouse_debit_amount`, against the Supplier (lines 250-269), plus LCV credits (271-291) and subcontracting credits (293-317). 3. Supplier is still credited the full billed total (`make_supplier_gl_entry`). ### Summary of the difference | | Update Stock OFF (vs PR) | Update Stock ON | |---|---|---| | Stock Ledger Entries | none | posted by the invoice | | Inventory debit | none | standard cost (SLE-forced) | | PPV | none — already on the PR | booked here by `make_stock_adjustment_entry` | | Expense-side debit | `Stock Received But Not Billed` = billed amount (clears the PR's credit) | `item.expense_account` = inventory account | In short: with Update Stock off the invoice never touches a P&L expense or PPV account — it debits only "Stock Received But Not Billed" to reverse the PR's booking, leaving the standard-cost inventory value and the purchase-price variance exactly as the Purchase Receipt posted them.

## The pattern: append a unique tiebreaker key to the ORDER BY Every "pick the latest row" query in ERPNext is written with **a secondary sort key that is unique per row — `creation` (row creation timestamp) and/or `name` (the document's unique primary key)** — appended after the date column, in the same direction: ```sql order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 ``` or in query-builder form: ```python .orderby(sle_entry.posting_date, order=frappe.qb.desc) .orderby(sle_entry.creation, order=frappe.qb.desc) .orderby(sle_entry.name, order=frappe.qb.desc) .limit(1) ``` This converts the ordering into a **total order**: rows that tie on the date column can no longer tie overall, so the single row returned by `LIMIT 1` is uniquely determined by the data rather than by the engine's arbitrary tie resolution. ## Why it matters across database engines The SQL standard leaves the order of tied rows undefined, so `ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1` with duplicate dates can return *different rows* on MariaDB vs PostgreSQL (different index/storage traversal). Both engines succeed — so a single-engine CI stays green — but a PostgreSQL site silently computes a different value. This repo classifies it as a **"silent divergence"** in the review guide **`.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md`** (§2): > **`ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` with no unique tiebreaker** — when rows tie on the ordered column the two engines may pick different rows. Add a `creation`/`name` tiebreaker **only if it does not change MariaDB's current pick** (see §4). Two governing constraints from that guide: - **MariaDB behaviour must not change** — the tiebreaker must reproduce MariaDB's current pick; if adding one would change MariaDB's result, or the engines already agree, it is deliberately *not* added (§4 "false positives"). - The tiebreaker interacts with the **NULL-ordering divergence** (MariaDB sorts `NULL` first, PostgreSQL last), so nullable date keys get a `Coalesce`/`isnull()` leading key first. The static guard `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` (docstring, lines 8–11) explicitly declares it **cannot** catch these `ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` tiebreaker cases — they're semantic, so they're covered by the guide, Greptile review config (`.greptile/config.json`), and targeted tests. ## Where it is applied — concrete functions **Stock ledger (valuation-critical):** - `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` — `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos()` (line 1627): `.orderby(posting_date, desc).orderby(creation, desc).orderby(name, desc).limit(1)` (lines 1653–1656), covered by `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py` (line 52, docstring explains "posting_date alone is non-total … creation/name tie-breaks make the latest SLE win identically on both engines"). - Same file — `get_stock_ledger_entries()` (line 1994) emits `order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}` (line 2071), which `get_previous_sle()` (line 1973) and the caller at line 1825 use with `limit 1` (and `for update`); the SLE-before-datetime query at line 1959 uses `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update`; the future-negative-qty checks use `over (order by posting_datetime, creation)` / `.orderby(posting_datetime).orderby(creation).limit(1)` (lines 2438–2440, 2450–2463). The dedicated regression test is `test_tie_breaking` (line 1132 in the same test file), which forces two SLEs to share `posting_date` + `posting_time` and asserts the `creation`-ordered result. - `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py` — `get_balance_qty_from_sle()` (line 77): `order_by="posting_datetime desc, creation desc", limit=1`; another lookup at line 322 uses `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc`. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reconciliation/test_stock_reconciliation.py` (lines 1128, 1167): `order_by="posting_time desc, creation desc"` in repost-verification helpers. **Item price / cost / closing:** - `erpnext/stock/get_item_details.py` — `get_item_price()` (line 1216): the comment at lines 1265–1267 ("Final unique tiebreaker: rows tied on every sort key above … MariaDB and Postgres can differ. Pin the pick.") closes the multi-key chain with `.orderby(ip.name, desc)`; the leading `.orderby(ip.valid_from.isnull())` normalizes the NULL-first/NULL-last divergence. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py` — `get_last_standard_cost()` (line 255): `order_by="effective_date desc, creation desc", limit=1`. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py` — `get_last_stock_closing_entry()` (line 340): `order_by="to_date desc, creation desc", limit=1`. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/serial_and_batch_bundle.py` — `get_stock_ledgers_for_serial_nos()` (line 3408): `.orderby(posting_datetime).orderby(creation)`, with the comment at line 3426 noting `creation` must also be *selected* because PostgreSQL requires ORDER BY columns in the select list for `DISTINCT` queries. **Accounts / selling / regional:** - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py` — `get_open_payment_requests_for_references()` (line 2770): `.orderby(Coalesce(transaction_date, creation)).orderby(creation).orderby(name)` with the comment "unique tiebreaker so PRs sharing a transaction_date allocate in the same order on both engines" (lines 2799–2801). - `erpnext/accounts/report/gross_profit/gross_profit.py` — the last-purchase-rate lookup (lines 905–909): `.orderby(posting_date, desc).orderby(name, desc).limit(1)`, and the payment-terms query at line 1017. - `erpnext/setup/utils.py` — `get_exchange_rate()` (line ~97): `order_by="date desc, name desc", limit=1` on Currency Exchange. - `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py` — `get_payer_address_html()` (line 126) and `get_street_address_html()` (line 147): `.orderby(address.name)` / `.orderby(link.parent)` tagged "deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"; I have the full picture. Here's the complete answer. ## The pattern: total-order tie-breaking after the date key Every "latest row" pick (`ORDER BY <date> DESC ... LIMIT 1`) in ERPNext appends secondary sort keys — `creation DESC` and/or the primary key `name DESC` — after the date column, making the sort key a **total order** so exactly one row wins even when several rows share the same date. It appears in three syntactic forms: - **`frappe.get_all` / raw SQL** — comma-extended `order_by`, e.g. `"posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"` (`erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:322`) or `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1959`) - **pypika (`frappe.qb`)** — chained `.orderby()` calls, e.g. `.orderby(sle_entry.posting_date, order=frappe.qb.desc).orderby(sle_entry.creation, ...).orderby(sle_entry.name, ...).limit(1)` (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1653–1656`) - **Priority-then-name** — `Case()` ranking first, then `name` as the final tie-break (`erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:132–134`) The code's own comments state the intent explicitly: `stock_balance.py:321` — *"total order so the latest SLE is picked identically on both engines (was posting_date only)"*; `irs_1099.py:134` — *"deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"*; `payment_entry.py:2799` — *"unique tiebreaker so PRs sharing a transaction_date allocate in the same order on both engines"*. ## Why it matters across database engines SQL does not define row ordering among rows that tie on the ORDER BY key, and `LIMIT 1` over a tie-set is resolved by whatever plan the engine happens to pick — so MariaDB and PostgreSQL (which ERPNext's CI runs on) can return **different rows** for the identical query. The test `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:52–98`) documents it precisely: > *"posting_date alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different incoming_rate could be resolved differently on MariaDB vs Postgres. creation/name tie-breaks make the latest SLE win identically on both engines."* This is business-critical, not cosmetic: the same-date tie decides which `incoming_rate` values a serialized item's stock valuation (`get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos`), or which Payment Request gets allocated first. Enforcement is layered: `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` (a pre-commit hook) explicitly declares *"ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers"* a **semantic** divergence it deliberately does *not* catch mechanically (lines 8–11) — that's left to the code comments, the dedicated tests (`test_stock_ledger_entry.py`, `test_irs_1099.py:16`, `erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py:12–14`), and reviewer convention. A Postgres-specific wrinkle also shows up in `serial_and_batch_bundle.py:3426–3433`: when the query is `DISTINCT`, the tiebreaker column (`creation`) must be added to the SELECT list too, because Postgres requires ORDER BY columns to appear in the select list. ## Where it is applied — concrete functions **Stock valuation (highest stakes):** - `UpdateEntriesAfter.get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos` — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1627–1661` — `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` + `limit 1` - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1929–1970` — raw SQL `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update` - `get_valuation_rate` path — `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:2162–2163`; also `:2336–2337`, `:2438–2439` (ascending "next row" picks) - `get_balance_qty_from_sle` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:77–86` — `posting_datetime desc, creation desc` - `set_stock_balance_as_per_serial_no` — `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:291–360` (query at `:317–325`, comment at `:321`) — `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` - `ItemStandardCost.get_last_standard_cost` (`:255–268`) and module-level `get_item_standard_rate` (`:291–311`) — `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py` — `effective_date desc, creation desc` + `limit 1` - Serial/batch valuation: `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py:537–538` and `erpnext/stock/deprecated_serial_batch.py:342–343` — `posting_datetime desc, creation desc` - `bom.py` latest-SLE rate lookup — `erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/bom/bom.py:1159–1160` - `StockReconciliation` previous-SLE read — `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reconciliation/stock_reconciliation.py:1229–1230` **Assets, CRM, setup, accounts:** - `AssetMovement.get_latest_location_and_custodian` — `erpnext/assets/doctype/asset_movement/asset_movement.py:128–151` — `transaction_date desc, name desc` + `.limit(1)` - `get_last_interaction` — `erpnext/crm/doctype/utils.py:6–45` — orders by `creation` alone (unique per row), backed by `erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py` - `get_exchange_rate` — `erpnext/setup/utils.py:97–103` — `date desc, name desc` + `limit 1` on Currency Exchange - Payment Request allocation order — `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py:2791–2802` — `Coalesce(transaction_date, creation) asc, creation asc, name asc` - `RepostAccountingLedger.validate_for_closed_fiscal_year` and `get_closing_balance_as_per_statement` — `erpnext/accounts/.../repost_accounting_ledger.py:46–71`, `erpnext/accounts/doctype/bank_account/bank_account.py:182–196` - Reports: `erpnext/accounts/report/bank_clearance_summary/bank_clearance_summary.py:98–149`, `erpnext/accounts/report/gross_profit/gross_profit.py:906–907`, `erpnext/accounts/doctype/exchange_rate_revaluation/exchange_rate_revaluation.py:661–677`, `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:126–161` Tests lock the behavior in by asserting against the tie-broken ordering itself (`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry/test_stock_entry.py:51`, `erpnext/stock/report/stock_balance/test_stock_balance.py:55`, `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_reconciliation/test_stock_reconciliation.py:1128,1167`), and `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py:345` (`to_date desc, creation desc`) applies the same convention for period-closing picks.

final answer
I now have the complete picture. Here is the full answer. ## The pattern: turn the sort into a *total order* before `LIMIT 1` Every "pick the latest row" query in this codebase follows the same three-layer sort key: 1. **Business date, `DESC`** — `posting_date` / `posting_datetime` / `transaction_date` / `effective_date` / `to_date` 2. **`creation DESC`** — first tie-breaker: a monotonic, effectively-unique timestamp that preserves "newest wins" semantics when two rows share the date 3. **`name DESC`** — the primary key, added when `creation` itself can tie (bulk inserts in the same timestamp tick), making the ordering a *total order* so `LIMIT 1` has exactly one well-defined winner In `frappe.qb` code it appears as chained `.orderby()` calls; in `frappe.get_all` as a comma-separated `order_by` string; in raw SQL as a comma-separated `ORDER BY`. A variant uses a `CASE()` precedence ordinal as the first key with `name` as the tie-break (IRS 1099 addresses). ## Why it matters across engines SQL never defines which row wins among ties on the sort key — MariaDB's InnoDB typically yields ties in index/heap order while Postgres' planner may pick a different physical order, so **the same data can return a different row** depending on the engine. ERPNext runs production on MariaDB but the test suite (label-gated Postgres job) on Postgres too, and an engine-dependent pick can change *business data*, not just report cosmetics — e.g. a different incoming rate for a transferred serial number changes the item's valuation between engines. The repo codifies this in **`.github/helper/postgres_compat.py`** (docstring, lines 8–11): the pre-commit hook only flags *mechanical* MySQL-isms; **"ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers"** are explicitly listed as *semantic* divergences that only the test suite or a human reviewer can catch. So enforcement is via tests that deliberately construct same-date ties and assert the identical winner on both engines. ## Where it is applied | Function | File / line | Sort key | |---|---|---| | `StockLedger.get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos` | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1627` (query at 1653–1656) | `.orderby(posting_date, desc).orderby(creation, desc).orderby(name, desc).limit(1)` — picks the incoming rate of a serial transferred to another company | | `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` | `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:1929` (SQL at 1959–1961) | raw SQL `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update` — previous SLE during reposting/valuation | | `get_balance_qty_from_sle` | `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:77–86` | `order_by="posting_datetime desc, creation desc", limit=1` | | Serial-balance correction query | `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py:317–325` | `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc", limit=1` — comment: *"total order so the latest SLE is picked identically on both engines (was posting_date only)"* | | `ItemStandardCost.get_last_standard_cost` and `get_item_standard_rate` | `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py:255–268, 290–309` | `order_by="effective_date desc, creation desc", limit=1` — latest submitted standard cost | | `StockClosingEntry.get_last_stock_closing_entry` | `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py:340–349` | `order_by="to_date desc, creation desc", limit=1` — carry-forward opening balances | | `AssetMovement.get_latest_location_and_custodian` | `erpnext/assets/doctype/asset_movement/asset_movement.py:128–151` | `.orderby(asm.transaction_date, desc).orderby(asm.name, desc).limit(1)` — current asset location/custodian | | `get_payer_address_html` / `get_street_address_html` | `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py:126–161` | CASE precedence (Postal > Billing) then `.orderby(address.name)` / `.orderby(link.parent)` — commented *"deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines"* | | `get_last_interaction` / `get_last_issue_from_customer` | `erpnext/crm/doctype/utils.py:6–57` | `order_by="creation desc", limit=1` — `creation` alone is accepted here because it is unique for Communication/Issue | ## Enforcement in tests - **`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:52–98`** — `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic`: docstring states *"posting_date alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different incoming_rate could be resolved differently on MariaDB vs Postgres."* It inserts `MAT-SLE-TIE-A` (rate 100) and `MAT-SLE-TIE-B` (rate 200) with the **same `posting_date`** — "later/larger name -> deterministic winner" — and asserts `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos` returns **200.0 on both engines**. - **`erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/test_irs_1099.py`** — asserts "the Postal address must win over the Billing one (deterministically, on both engines)" when several addresses share the top precedence tier. - **`erpnext/crm/doctype/test_utils.py:11–14`** — `test_get_last_interaction_for_contact` documents that "`creation` is unique, so the LIMIT-1 pick is deterministic and identical on MariaDB and Postgres", pinning the single-key variant. - Related determinism fixes in the same spirit (same root cause, ordering/grouping rather than LIMIT-1) appear in `erpnext/selling/report/sales_order_analysis/sales_order_analysis.py:46–52` (uses `nowdate()` instead of DB `CURRENT_DATE`, groups on the PK) and `erpnext/accounts/report/sales_register/sales_register.py:491` / `purchase_register.py:461` (`.orderby("name", order=Order.desc)` as the final key). **In short:** the guarantee is a deterministic total sort — business date DESC → `creation` DESC → unique `name` DESC — appended before `LIMIT 1` at every "latest row" pick, because ties are resolved arbitrarily and *differently* by MariaDB and Postgres; the repo enforces it not in the static `postgres_compat.py` hook (which explicitly declines to catch it) but with same-date-tie test fixtures asserting identical winners on both engines.

final answer
## Summary ERPNext's stock reposting/valuation stack (this codebase) handles Postgres concurrency with a layered scheme: **RQ job deduplication → Postgres advisory locks (session-level for repost-vs-repost, transaction-scoped for stock writes and batch valuation) → `FOR UPDATE` row locks as the correctness layer → deterministic ordering + recoverable-error re-queueing**. Here is exactly where each piece lives. ### 1. Per-(item, warehouse) repost gate — prevents repost-vs-repost deadlock `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`: - `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300` (line 273) — deliberately well under the 1800 s repost job timeout. - `repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)` (line 276) — on Postgres returns `frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`; a **session-level** advisory lock taken *before* any row locks, so two background reposts of the same `(item_code, warehouse)` take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock. On MariaDB (or an older frappe without `advisory_lock`, checked via `hasattr`) it degrades to `nullcontext()`. The tuple key is used so `:` in names can't collide two pairs onto one lock. - `repost_future_sle()` (line 304) wraps each item-warehouse chunk in `with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse):` → `update_entries_after(...)` (line 335). Crucially, the gate is **session-level** because the repost loop commits mid-run (`update_data_in_repost`, lines 885–887, and `update_args_in_repost_item_valuation`, line 408, both call `frappe.db.commit()` to checkpoint progress for resume). The synchronous submit path (`repost_current_voucher` → `make_sl_entries`) is deliberately *not* gated — blocking a submit behind a background repost would be worse; it relies on the row locks + deadlock retry instead (docstring, lines 276–283). ### 2. Transaction-scoped write gate — prevents lost updates on Postgres `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`: - `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)` (line 292) — `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse), timeout=300)`. MariaDB's gap locks from its previous-SLE locking reads block concurrent inserts; **Postgres has no gap locks and locking reads don't see other transactions' uncommitted inserts**, so without this two writers could compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's Bin write would be lost. It's txn-scoped and re-entrant, released at commit/rollback. - Taken in `make_sl_entries()` (lines 117–120) for **sorted** `{(item_code, warehouse)}` pairs — sorting guarantees two vouchers touching overlapping pairs can't acquire the gates in opposite order (no lock-order inversion) — and again in `update_entries_after.__init__` (line 613). ### 3. Batch average-rate computation — prevents double-computing `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, `class BatchNoValuation`: - `calculate_avg_rate()` (line 818) — for an **outward** SLE (`actual_qty <= 0`), on Postgres it first takes `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse))` (lines 824–831) *before* reading the batch history in `get_batch_stock_before_date()` (line 847). - Why an advisory lock here: the history aggregate is a `GROUP BY batch_no` query, and `FOR UPDATE` is **invalid with GROUP BY on Postgres** — so `get_batch_stock_before_date` only calls `.for_update()` when `frappe.db.db_type != "postgres"` (lines 894–895). On MariaDB the grouped row lock serializes; on Postgres the txn-scoped advisory lock serializes concurrent valuations of the same `(item, warehouse)` so only one transaction reads the batch totals and writes `stock_value_difference`/`incoming_rate` back to `Serial and Batch Entry`. - The legacy path does the same: `erpnext/stock/deprecated_serial_batch.py`, `DeprecatedBatchNoValuation.get_sle_for_batches()` skips `.for_update()` on Postgres (lines 159–160) and relies on the caller's `("batch-valuation", …)` lock (comments at lines 147–148, 269, 397, and `serial_batch_bundle.py:882`). ### 4. Row `FOR UPDATE` locks — the correctness layer that still applies `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`: - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher()` — raw SQL ending in `for update` (line 1961) pins the last SLE before the repost point. - `get_future_entries_to_repost()` (line 904) / `get_sle_after_datetime()` (line 1831) — `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., ">=", "asc", for_update=True)`, i.e. all future SLEs being re-valuated are row-locked, so no other transaction can re-post the same rows even if it slipped past the gates. ### 5. Job scheduling — avoids duplicate/overlapping background jobs `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`: - `enqueue_reposting_entry()` (line 828) — `frappe.enqueue(..., queue="long", timeout=1800, job_id=f"repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}", deduplicate=True)`: the same `Repost Item Valuation` can't be enqueued twice. - `run_parallel_reposting()` (line 791) — bounded by `Stock Reposting Settings.no_of_parallel_reposting` (default 4); skips entries with live RQ jobs (`get_entries_with_active_jobs`, line 850) and **skips items that already have an active repost job** (`get_items_with_active_reposting`, line 860), so two workers never repost the same item concurrently in the first place. - `repost()` (line 530) — `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (line 36); on those, status stays `"In Progress"` and the entry is re-queued instead of failing permanently (lines 577–592). The comment explicitly notes this catches Postgres's `"deadlock detected"` (the old MariaDB-only traceback match missed it). The 300 s lock timeout surfaces as a recoverable `QueryTimeoutError`, freeing the worker slot. - Deterministic ordering: `get_items_to_be_repost()` (stock_ledger.py, line 478) returns item-warehouse pairs grouped by `item_code, warehouse` ordered by `creation asc`, and `sort_sles()` (line 803) orders by `(posting_datetime, creation)` — consistent ordering across workers. ### 6. Concurrent Bin inserts `erpnext/stock/utils.py`, `_create_bin()` (line 227) — insert inside a savepoint; on `frappe.UniqueValidationError` it rolls back **to the savepoint only** (required to keep the Postgres transaction usable) and re-reads the winner's Bin. ### Regression tests - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py::test_stock_write_takes_sle_advisory_gate` (line 37) - `erpnext/stock/doctype/serial_and_batch_bundle/test_serial_and_batch_bundle.py::test_outward_batch_valuation_takes_transaction_advisory_lock` (line 204) Both assert via `SELECT count(*) FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory' AND pid = pg_backend_pid()` that the gate is actually held on Postgres. **In short:** for the same item-warehouse batch, background reposts serialize on the session-level `stock_repost` advisory lock (with a 300 s bounded wait), every stock write serializes on the txn-scoped `stock-sle` lock, batch average-rate computation serializes on the txn-scoped `batch-valuation` lock (replacing MariaDB's grouped `FOR UPDATE`, which Postgres cannot do with `GROUP BY`), `FOR UPDATE` row locks on the previous/future SLE history remain the correctness backstop, gate acquisition is order-normalized, and anything that still deadlocks or times out is classified as `RecoverableErrors` and re-queued as "In Progress" rather than double-computing or failing.

final answer
## Short answer On Postgres, the subsystem replaces MariaDB's gap-lock behavior with **per-(item, warehouse) Postgres advisory locks** layered under the existing `FOR UPDATE` row locks, plus **RIV (Repost Item Valuation) job deduplication and recoverable-retry semantics**. There are three distinct gates, all Postgres-only (`frappe.db.db_type == "postgres"`, guarded by `hasattr` so older frappe falls back gracefully): ## 1. `repost_gate` — serializes repost-vs-repost before row locks (deadlock prevention) `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:276-289`, with `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300` (line 273). ```python def repost_gate(item_code, warehouse): if frappe.db.db_type == "postgres" and hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock"): return frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT) return nullcontext() ``` - It's a **session-level advisory lock** keyed by the tuple `("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse)` (tuple key so a colon in a name can't collide two pairs onto one lock). It's taken in `repost_future_sle` (line 335) around each per-item-warehouse `update_entries_after(...)` call, **before** the inner `... for update` row locks, so two concurrent background reposts of the same pair *take turns* instead of acquiring the same row locks in different orders and deadlocking. Row locks still enforce correctness; the gate only cuts deadlock/retry churn. - The 300 s timeout is deliberately under the 1800 s repost job timeout, so a contended worker gives up, re-queues (recoverable `QueryTimeoutError`), and frees the slot instead of pinning it. - Scope is intentionally **repost-vs-repost only** — the synchronous `repost_current_voucher` submit path is *not* gated (blocking a user submit behind a background repost would be a worse regression) and keeps relying on deadlock retry. MariaDB keeps the plain deadlock-retry path. ## 2. `sle_processing_gate` — serializes all stock writes per (item, warehouse) `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:292-301`, using the **transaction-scoped, re-entrant** `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`, released at commit/rollback. - Called in `make_sl_entries` (line 120) — on the **sorted** set of pairs, so two vouchers touching the same item-warehouse pairs can't take the gates in opposite order (line 118-119) — and in `update_entries_after.__init__` (line 613), the reposting valuation entry point. - Reason: Postgres locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting (no gap locks like MariaDB), so without this gate two concurrent writers would compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's Bin write would be lost. ## 3. `("batch-valuation", item, warehouse)` — the double-computation guard for batch average rate `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py:818-831`, in `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate()` (the class extending `DeprecatedBatchNoValuation`; the same design is documented in `erpnext/stock/deprecated_serial_batch.py:148, 269, 397`): ```python if frappe.db.db_type == "postgres": frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock( ("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse) ) entries = self.get_batch_stock_before_date() ``` - On **outward** batch SLEs, the batch average rate is recomputed from the SLE/bundle history via grouped queries (`get_batch_stock_before_date`, `calculate_avg_rate_from_deprecarated_ledgers`). On MariaDB those queries carry `FOR UPDATE` + gap locks; on **Postgres `FOR UPDATE` is invalid with `GROUP BY`**, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple. So the grouped history queries explicitly skip `.for_update()` on Postgres (`serial_batch_bundle.py:894-895`, `deprecated_serial_batch.py:159-160, 292-293`) and the txn-scoped advisory lock serializes the whole read-modify-write instead — two concurrent valuations of the same (item, warehouse) batches can't both compute from the same snapshot and double-apply the stock-value difference. ## Orchestration-level protections (so jobs rarely contend at all) - **Job dedup**: `enqueue_reposting_entry` (`repost_item_valuation.py:828-837`) enqueues with `job_id=f"repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}"` and `deduplicate=True`; the parallel driver `run_parallel_reposting` (line 791, cron every 15 min via `hooks.py:463-468`, self-re-enqueued on completion) skips entries with active jobs (`get_entries_with_active_jobs`) and skips any "Item and Warehouse" repost whose `item_code` already has an active repost job (`get_items_with_active_reposting`), capped by `no_of_parallel_reposting` (default 4) from Stock Reposting Settings. - **Document-level dedup**: `deduplicate_similar_repost` (line 322) marks later-queued RIVs for the same item+warehouse as "Skipped"; `skip_reposts_covered_by_dependents`/`mark_covered_item_reposts` (lines 354-436) skip queued reposts already covered by a completed one; `has_pending_valuation_repost` (`stock_reposting_settings.py:316`) stops the weekly auto-repost from stacking duplicates. - **Deadlock is recoverable, not fatal**: `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (line 36) — `repost()`'s handler (lines 563-602) re-queues the RIV as "In Progress" instead of "Failed" (the comment notes the old traceback string-match missed Postgres "deadlock detected" and failed reposts permanently). - **Checkpoint/resume**: `update_args_in_repost_item_valuation` (`stock_ledger.py:368-408`) and `update_reposting_progress` persist `current_index`, `items_to_be_repost` and a gzipped reposting-data file (last-posted SLE per pair) and commit — "so if timeout happens, it can be resumed from the last posted voucher" (line 885-887) — so a job that times out waiting on a gate resumes rather than recomputing. - Correctness underneath is still enforced by the actual row locks: reposting locks future SLEs via `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., for_update=True)` (`get_future_entries_to_repost`, `stock_ledger.py:903-904`). In short: a session-level gate (`stock_repost`) orders concurrent repost jobs per item-warehouse to prevent lock-order deadlocks; a txn-scoped gate (`stock-sle`) serializes all stock writes per pair; a txn-scoped gate (`batch-valuation`) ensures only one transaction recomputes a batch's average rate at a time (replacing MariaDB's grouped `FOR UPDATE`/gap locks, which Postgres can't provide); and RIV job deduplication + recoverable-retry + checkpointed resume ensure duplicate or interrupted background jobs don't redo the same valuation.

final answer
I now have the full picture across the orchestration layer, the ledger engine, and the batch-valuation path. Here's the complete answer. ## Overview Backdated stock transactions don't repost synchronously — they create **Repost Item Valuation (RIV)** documents that background jobs drain (`erpnext/stock/spec/reposting.md`, `repost_entries()` / `run_parallel_reposting()` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`). Entry point per entry: `repost()` → `repost_sl_entries()` → `repost_future_sle()` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. On PostgreSQL the subsystem layers **three advisory-lock gates + `FOR UPDATE` row locks + job-level deduplication + recoverable-error re-queuing**; on MariaDB it relies on InnoDB gap locks and plain deadlock retry instead. ## 1. Deadlock prevention — `repost_gate()` (Postgres-only) `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:276-289`: - `repost_future_sle()` iterates item-warehouse pairs and wraps each recompute in `with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse):` (L335). On Postgres this takes a **session-level advisory lock** keyed `("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse)` with a 300s timeout (`REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT`, L273 — deliberately under the 1800s job timeout so a contended worker re-queues instead of burning its budget). - It's taken **before** the inner `... FOR UPDATE` row locks so two concurrent background reposts of the same item-warehouse *take turns* instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock. Row locks still enforce correctness; the gate only cuts deadlock/retry churn. - Scope is **repost-vs-repost only**: the synchronous `repost_current_voucher` submit path is deliberately not gated (blocking a user submit behind a background repost would be worse) and keeps relying on the framework's existing deadlock retry. - Graceful opt-in: `hasattr(frappe.db, "advisory_lock")` falls back to `nullcontext()` on older Frappe rather than permanently failing the RIV. ## 2. Lost-update prevention — `sle_processing_gate()` (txn-scoped, every stock write) `stock_ledger.py:292-301`: a **transaction-scoped, re-entrant** advisory lock `("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse)` (timeout 300s, released at commit/rollback). Taken at: - `make_sl_entries()` (L117-120) — for **every** stock write, over all (item, warehouse) pairs, **sorted** so two vouchers touching the same pairs can't take the gates in opposite order (another lock-order-deadlock guard); - `update_entries_after.__init__()` (L613) — before the reposting recompute. Why Postgres needs it: MariaDB's locking history reads take *gap locks* that both block and then reveal concurrent inserts. Postgres `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` does neither — locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting — so without this gate two concurrent writers would compute from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's `Bin` write would be silently lost. ## 3. The "average rate for the same item-warehouse batch valuation" guard `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`, `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate()` (L818-845): when valuing an **outward** entry (`actual_qty <= 0`), the batch-wise average rate is recomputed from history via `get_batch_stock_before_date()`. Before that read, on Postgres it takes `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", self.sle.item_code, self.sle.warehouse))` (L828-831). The comment is explicit: MariaDB's grouped `FOR UPDATE` + gap locks on the history reads do this job; Postgres has no gap locks, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple — the txn-scoped advisory lock serializes the valuation without either. So two jobs can never double-compute the batch average rate for the same item-warehouse. Backed by tests: `test_outward_batch_valuation_takes_transaction_advisory_lock` (`serial_and_batch_bundle` test, L204-229) and `test_stock_write_takes_sle_advisory_gate` (`stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py:37-50`, asserting `pg_locks` advisory count increases). ## 4. Correctness backstop — `FOR UPDATE` row locks The recompute itself (`update_entries_after.build()` → `repost_stock_ledgers()` → `repost_stock_ledger_entry()`, stock_ledger.py L709-810/836-841, then `update_bin()` L1891-1903) re-derives queue/qty/average rate from rows it holds locks on: - `get_future_entries_to_repost()` (L904) and `get_sle_after_datetime()` (L1831) call `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., for_update=True)`, which appends literal `for update` to the SQL (L2075); - `get_sle_against_current_voucher()` uses the query-builder `.for_update()` (L1920). ## 5. Never doing the work twice at the queue level - **RQ job dedup**: `enqueue_reposting_entry()` uses `job_id=f"repost_item_valuation_entry_{name}"` + `deduplicate=True` (L828-837); `get_entries_with_active_jobs()` scans started/pending RQ job IDs, and `get_items_with_active_reposting()` excludes any queued entry whose `item_code` already has an active job — so `run_parallel_reposting()` never starts two jobs on the same item (L791-825). - **Claim marker**: `repost()` sets status to "In Progress" and commits *before* doing work (L539-541). - **Superseding reposts**: after completion, `deduplicate_similar_repost()` (L322) marks later `Queued` RIVs for the same item-warehouse with a later posting datetime as "Skipped" (using portable `CombineDatetime`, explicitly avoiding MySQL-only `TIMESTAMP()`); `skip_reposts_covered_by_dependents()` + `mark_covered_item_reposts`/`mark_covered_transaction_reposts` skip reposts fully covered by a dependent one (coverage accumulated in the `riv_dependent_coverage::{name}` cache, L457-470). - **Resumability instead of recompute**: `update_data_in_repost()` commits progress (index, `items_to_be_repost`, `reposting_data_file`) every 2000 SLEs (stock_ledger.py L885-887), so a timed-out job resumes from the last posted voucher; `frappe.db.MAX_WRITES_PER_TRANSACTION *= 4` avoids mid-repost write-limit aborts. ## 6. Safety net — classify deadlocks as recoverable `repost_item_valuation.py` L36, L563-601: `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)`. On any of these, `repost()` rolls back, logs, and sets the RIV back to **"In Progress"** for the scheduler to retry — never "Failed". The comment records that the old traceback string-match only knew MariaDB's "Deadlock found" and **missed Postgres's "deadlock detected"**, failing reposts permanently; classification is now by exception type (verified by `test_repost_item_valuation.py:368-397`, asserting `QueryDeadlockError("deadlock detected")` → `"In Progress"`). A patch, `erpnext/patches/v13_0/requeue_recoverable_reposts.py`, repairs RIVs failed under the old scheme. **In short**: on Postgres, concurrent reposts are serialized per (item, warehouse) by a session-level advisory gate (`repost_gate`) before row locks to avoid lock-order deadlocks; all stock writes and batch-average-rate computations are serialized per (item, warehouse) by transaction-scoped advisory gates (`sle_processing_gate`, `("batch-valuation", ...)`), which substitutes for MariaDB's gap locks; `FOR UPDATE` reads of future SLEs plus the RQ job/item-level dedup and RIV skip logic ensure exactly one recompute of each average rate; and anything that still deadlocks or times out is re-queued as "In Progress" instead of failing.

All layers are now confirmed. Here's the complete picture. ## Overview On Postgres, ERPNext's reposting stack uses **four cooperating layers** — job-queue deduplication, Postgres advisory locks (session- and transaction-scoped), `FOR UPDATE` row locks, and checkpoint/resume with type-based error recovery. The Postgres-specific code lives in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`; the job machinery lives in `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`. ## 1. Job level — never run two background jobs on the same work **`enqueue_reposting_entry`** (`repost_item_valuation.py:828`) enqueues `execute_reposting_entry` on the `long` queue with `job_id=f"{REPOSTING_JOB_ID_PREFIX}{name}"` (`REPOSTING_JOB_ID_PREFIX = "repost_item_valuation_entry_"`, line 788) and `deduplicate=True` — one RQ job per `Repost Item Valuation` doc, maximum. **`run_parallel_reposting`** (`:791`, invoked every 15 min via `hooks.py` as a recovery net, then re-enqueued by each finished job in `execute_reposting_entry`'s `finally` block) adds two guards: - **`get_entries_with_active_jobs`** (`:850`) reads the live RQ queue (`get_queue("long")`, pending IDs + `started_job_registry.get_job_ids()`) and filters by the site-prefixed job-ID prefix, so it knows exactly which repost docs have queued/running jobs. - **`get_items_with_active_reposting`** (`:860`) turns those into a set of item codes currently being reposted. The enqueue loop (`:810-825`) skips any entry already in progress, skips any entry whose `item_code` is in that set, and only parallelizes `based_on == "Item and Warehouse"` entries — capped at `no_of_parallel_reposting` (default 4) **distinct items**, one entry each. So even with parallelism enabled, no two workers ever touch the same item, hence never the same (item, warehouse). ## 2. Postgres advisory locks — the deadlock gate and the write gate **`repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)`** (`stock_ledger.py:276`): on Postgres (`frappe.db.db_type == "postgres"`, with a `hasattr` graceful opt-in if frappe lacks `advisory_lock`; MariaDB gets a no-op `nullcontext()`), it takes a **session-level** advisory lock `frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`. It is acquired in **`repost_future_sle`** (`:335`) around each `update_entries_after(...)` construction. Per its docstring, the lock is taken *before* the inner `... FOR UPDATE` row locks so concurrent reposts of overlapping item-warehouse sets **take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock**; row locks still enforce correctness, the gate only cuts deadlock/retry churn. Scope is deliberately repost-vs-repost only — the synchronous submit path is not gated. The tuple key means a colon in item/warehouse names can't collide two distinct pairs onto one lock. Timeout is `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 300` (`:273`), kept under the 1800s job timeout so a contended worker times out, re-queues (recoverable), and frees its slot. **`sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)`** (`:292`): called inside `update_entries_after.__init__` (`:613`), this takes a **transaction-scoped, re-entrant** lock `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse), timeout=300)`. Its docstring explains why this is Postgres-only: MariaDB's locking reads take **gap locks** that also block then reveal concurrent inserts; **Postgres locking reads never see rows another transaction is inserting**. Without this gate, two concurrent writers (repost vs. a live submit, or another repost) would both seed from the same stale previous SLE and the loser's `Bin` write would be silently lost. This is the mechanism that prevents **double-computing the average rate**: only one transaction at a time may compute and write the running valuation state for a given (item, warehouse). ## 3. Row locks — the correctness backbone The average rate is computed in memory by `update_entries_after.process_sle` from the `stock_queue` / `valuation_rate` state carried in `self.prev_sle_dict`, seeded from the previous SLE. Two locked reads anchor that computation: - **`get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`** (`stock_ledger.py:1929`) — the seed query ends in `for update` (`:1961`), locking the anchor row. - **`update_entries_after.get_future_entries_to_repost`** (`:903`) — re-reads all future SLEs via `get_stock_ledger_entries(..., for_update=True)`. Within a single run, `repost_stock_ledgers` (`:767`) also deduplicates via `self.distinct_sles` ("To avoid duplicate reposting of same sle in case of multiple dependant sle", `:779-794`). ## 4. Recovery — a retry can't double-apply - **`repost()`** (`repost_item_valuation.py:530`) sets status `"In Progress"` and commits (`:539-541`) before working. On exceptions it classifies by **type** against `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)` (`:36`) and re-queues `"In Progress"` instead of `"Failed"` (`:577-580`) — the comment notes the old traceback string-match missed Postgres's `"deadlock detected"` (vs MariaDB's `"Deadlock found"`), so PG deadlocks used to fail permanently. - **Checkpoint/resume**: `repost_future_sle` tracks `current_index` and after each item-warehouse calls `update_args_in_repost_item_valuation` (`:359`), which gzips `{repost_affected_transaction, item_wh_wise_last_posted_sle, item_wh_first_reposted}` into the doc's `reposting_data_file` and commits (`:398-408`). `update_data_in_repost` (`stock_ledger.py:865`) similarly commits every 2000 SLEs so a timed-out job resumes from the last posted voucher rather than recomputing from scratch — the resumed `item_wh_wise_last_posted_sle` state is also what keeps the recomputation anchored instead of diverging. - **Final sweep**: `_execute_reposting_entry` (`:896`) only processes docs in status `Queued`/`In Progress`, skips accounting-only reposts whose `reposting_reference` hasn't Completed, then `doc.deduplicate_similar_repost()` (`:322`) marks overlapping reposts as `Skipped`. **In short**: the RQ job-ID dedup + active-job/item exclusion guarantees at most one worker per item; the Postgres session advisory lock (`stock_repost` key) turns concurrent reposts into a serial queue before row locks are touched, eliminating the lock-order deadlock; the transaction-scoped advisory lock (`stock-sle` key) plus `FOR UPDATE` reads of the previous/future SLEs guarantee only one transaction computes-and-writes the running average rate per (item, warehouse) — compensating for Postgres lacking MariaDB's gap-lock behavior; and type-based `RecoverableErrors` re-queuing plus the gzipped checkpoint file make any timeout/deadlock retry resume idempotently instead of double-computing.

final answer
I have everything needed. The mechanism is row-level locking via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, plus a status state machine and a "Running" gate in the worker. ## The locking mechanism: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` When a Period Closing Voucher is submitted, `PeriodClosingVoucher.on_submit()` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/period_closing_voucher/period_closing_voucher.py`) creates a **Process Period Closing Voucher (PPCV)** document. Its `validate()` → `populate_processing_tables()` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`) splits the period into one child row per (date, report_type) pair in the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` child table (`normal_balances` = one "Profit and Loss" + one "Balance Sheet" row per day; `z_opening_balances` = one "Balance Sheet" row per day if it's the first PCV). Each row starts as `status="Queued"`. The critical mutual-exclusion logic lives in two functions in `process_period_closing_voucher.py`: **1. `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)`** — the initial fan-out (up to 4 workers at once): ```python qb.from_(ppcvd) .select(ppcvd.name, ppcvd.processing_date, ppcvd.report_type, ppcvd.parentfield) .where(ppcvd.parent.eq(docname) & ppcvd.status.eq("Queued")) .orderby(ppcvd.parentfield, ppcvd.idx, ppcvd.processing_date) .limit(threads) # threads = 4 .for_update(skip_locked=True) # <-- the guarantee .run(as_dict=True) ``` **2. `schedule_next_date(docname)`** — the chaining call each worker makes after finishing a row, using the same query with `.limit(1)`. `for_update(skip_locked=True)` translates to SQL `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. When two workers run this query concurrently, the database row-level lock means: - If worker A's transaction already holds a lock on a (date, report_type) row it claimed, worker B's query **skips that row entirely instead of waiting**, and claims the next unlocked `Queued` row. So no two workers can ever claim the same row. - There's no blocking or lock-wait contention; workers just move on to the next available row. ## Locking is made durable before dispatching the job Grabbing the lock alone wouldn't be enough, because the row lock only lasts until the claiming transaction commits. The code handles this explicitly: 1. Immediately after the `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` select, each claimed row is flipped to `status="Running"` via `frappe.db.set_value(...)`. 2. An explicit **`frappe.db.commit()`** is issued right away ("keep transaction on PPCV and PPCVD short / prevents concurrency errors - REPEATABLE READ"), so the row claim is committed and the lock is released while the status is already `Running` — long before the heavy aggregation runs. 3. Only then is `process_individual_date` enqueued with **`enqueue_after_commit=True`**, guaranteeing the background job is only created after the `Running` claim is durable in the DB. ## The worker-side gate: `process_individual_date` As a second safety layer, the background job itself re-validates its claim before doing any work: ```python def process_individual_date(docname, row_name, date, report_type, parentfield): current_date_status = frappe.db.get_value( "Process Period Closing Voucher Detail", row_name, "status" ) if current_date_status != "Running": return # bails out if the row was paused/cancelled/re-claimed meanwhile ``` It then does its per-day aggregation (GL sums grouped by account + dimensions for that date and report type), writes the result to the row's `closing_balance` JSON field, sets the row to `Completed`, commits, and calls `schedule_next_date(docname)` — which claims the next `Queued` row with the same `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` query, keeping every worker fed. When no `Queued` rows remain and all rows are `Completed`, the final `summarize_and_post_ledger_entries` job (guarded against duplicates by the `is_job_running(f"summarize_{docname}")` check and a fixed `job_name`) consolidates the per-date balances and posts the actual GL/closing entries. ## Supporting details - **Performance of the claim query**: `on_doctype_update()` in `process_period_closing_voucher_detail.py` adds a composite index on `(parent, status, parentfield, idx, processing_date)` so the locked `SELECT` scans efficiently. - **State machine**: rows go `Queued → Running → Completed`, with `Paused`/`Cancelled` handled by `pause_pcv_processing`/`cancel_pcv_processing`/`resume_pcv_processing`; the "Running" gate in the worker ensures a paused/cancelled row isn't processed even if a job was already enqueued. - These are the **only two uses of `skip_locked`** in the entire ERPNext codebase, confirming this is the designated concurrency-control mechanism for PCV processing. **In short:** mutual exclusion is enforced at claim time by a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` query over the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` rows filtered to `status="Queued"` — a row already locked (claimed) by another worker's transaction is skipped rather than blocked — combined with immediately committing the row's `Queued → Running` flip, enqueuing the job only after that commit (`enqueue_after_commit=True`), and a worker-side re-check that the row is still `Running` before processing.

## Answer The mechanism is a **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` row-claiming query** on the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` child table — each background worker atomically "claims" a date/report-type row under a database row lock before processing it. ### The full flow **1. Splitting the work into rows** — `PeriodClosingVoucher.on_submit` (`erpnext/accounts/doctype/period_closing_voucher/period_closing_voucher.py:135-141`) creates and submits a `Process Period Closing Voucher` (PPCV) helper document (unless `use_legacy_controller_for_pcv` is set). Its `validate()` → `populate_processing_tables()` → `generate_pcv_dates()` expands the PCV period into one child row **per (processing_date, report_type)** in the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` table — two rows per day ("Profit and Loss" and "Balance Sheet"), all with `status = "Queued"` (`process_period_closing_voucher.py:55-67`). If it's the first PCV, `generate_opening_balances_dates()` (lines 69–83) additionally queues `z_opening_balances` rows (Balance Sheet, `is_opening = "Yes"` GL entries) for every date between the earliest and latest GL posting date. **2. Atomic row claiming** — `on_submit` → `start_pcv_processing(docname)` → `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)` (lines 92–133): ```python qb.from_(ppcvd) .select(ppcvd.name, ppcvd.processing_date, ppcvd.report_type, ppcvd.parentfield) .where(ppcvd.parent.eq(docname) & ppcvd.status.eq("Queued")) .orderby(ppcvd.parentfield, ppcvd.idx, ppcvd.processing_date) .limit(threads) # threads = 4 .for_update(skip_locked=True) # ← the concurrency guarantee .run(as_dict=True) ``` This compiles to `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. If multiple worker transactions run this query at the same time, the database grants row locks to the first transaction that touches a row; **every other worker's `SKIP LOCKED` query silently skips those locked rows** and returns only still-unlocked "Queued" rows. So no two workers can ever claim the same date/report-type row — and unlike a plain `FOR UPDATE`, a worker never blocks waiting on another; it just picks different rows. Immediately after selection, each claimed row's status is flipped to `"Running"`. **3. Lock-window minimization** — each job is enqueued with `enqueue_after_commit=True`, and the scheduler does an explicit `frappe.db.commit()` right after marking rows "Running" (line 131, with the comment *"keep transaction on PPCV and PPCVD short — prevents concurrency errors - REPEATABLE READ"*). This releases the row locks fast and guarantees the `"Running"` status is committed and visible **before** the `process_individual_date` job ever starts — so a job never begins on a row still showing `"Queued"` to other workers. **4. Defense in depth in the worker** — `process_individual_date` (lines 543–610) re-reads its row's status and returns immediately if it isn't `"Running"` (lines 544–550), guarding against races with pause/cancel or duplicate enqueues. After aggregating GL balances for that date/report type, it stores the JSON result, sets the row to `"Completed"`, commits, and then chains `schedule_next_date(docname)`. **5. Work chaining with the same primitive** — `schedule_next_date` (lines 256–320) claims the *next* single "Queued" row using the identical `.for_update(skip_locked=True)` pattern (line 266, `limit(1)`), commits, and enqueues the next job. When no "Queued" rows remain, it verifies `total_no_of_dates == completed` and enqueues `summarize_and_post_ledger_entries` — protected against duplicate summarize jobs by the `is_job_running(f"summarize_{docname}")` check. ### Summary Concurrency safety comes from **database-level row locking, not application locks or Redis**: the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` row *is* the work-queue item, and `.for_update(skip_locked=True)` turns claiming a row into an atomic, non-blocking operation. Status transitions (`Queued` → `Running` → `Completed`/`Paused`/`Cancelled`, managed by `start_pcv_processing`, `pause_pcv_processing`, `cancel_pcv_processing`, `resume_pcv_processing`) are persisted and committed before/after the locked section, with the worker-side "must be Running" re-check as a second line of defense.

## Answer The guarantee comes from **database row-level locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`**, combined with a `Queued → Running → Completed` status state machine on the child-table rows. All of this lives in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`. ### The setup (work is split into rows) When a PCV is submitted (and the legacy controller isn't used), `PeriodClosingVoucher.on_submit()` (`period_closing_voucher.py:135-141`) creates a `Process Period Closing Voucher` (PPCV) doc. Its `validate()` → `populate_processing_tables()` builds the work units: - `generate_pcv_dates()` (line 55) appends **one child row per (processing_date × report_type)** — every date in the period gets two rows in the `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail` child table (`normal_balances`): one for `"Profit and Loss"`, one for `"Balance Sheet"`, each with `status = "Queued"`. - `generate_opening_balances_dates()` (line 69) adds Balance Sheet rows to `z_opening_balances` covering the earliest GL posting date if it's the first PCV. ### The mutual-exclusion mechanism Work is claimed by two entry points — `initialize_parallel_threads()` (line 92, initial batch of `threads = 4`) and `schedule_next_date()` (line 256, chained one-at-a-time after each row completes). Both use the identical claiming query: ```python qb.from_(ppcvd) .select(ppcvd.name, ppcvd.processing_date, ppcvd.report_type, ppcvd.parentfield) .where(ppcvd.parent.eq(docname) & ppcvd.status.eq("Queued")) .orderby(ppcvd.parentfield, ppcvd.idx, ppcvd.processing_date) .limit(threads) # limit(1) in schedule_next_date .for_update(skip_locked=True) # <-- the key line .run(as_dict=True) ``` How this prevents two workers from grabbing the same row: 1. **`FOR UPDATE`** takes exclusive row locks on the candidate rows inside the claiming worker's transaction. 2. **`SKIP LOCKED`** makes concurrent claimers silently skip rows already locked by another worker's transaction — so when two workers race, the same `(processing_date, report_type)` row can only be returned to one of them; the other's query just doesn't see it. This is the classic "job queue claim" pattern (no lock waits, no duplicates). 3. The winner immediately flips the row's `status` to **`"Running"`** via `frappe.db.set_value`, then commits right away — the code comments explicitly say *"keep transaction on PPCV and PPCVD short / prevents concurrency errors - REPEATABLE READ"* (lines 128-131 and 276-279). Once committed and `Running`, the row no longer matches the `status.eq("Queued")` filter for any future claim. 4. The background job is enqueued with **`enqueue_after_commit=True`** (queue `"long"`, timeout from `Accounts Settings.pcv_job_timeout`), so the RQ job can't even start before the "Running" status is durably committed. 5. As a second layer of defense, the worker function `process_individual_date()` (line 543) re-reads the row's status and **returns early if it isn't `"Running"`** — protecting against stale/duplicated jobs (e.g., after a pause/cancel raced with enqueue). 6. After computing the grouped GL sums for that date/report type and storing them in the row's `closing_balance` JSON field, it sets `status = "Completed"`, commits, and **chains** `schedule_next_date()` to claim the next row — repeating the same locked claim. When no `Queued` rows remain and all rows are `Completed`, the final `summarize_and_post_ledger_entries()` is enqueued (guarded by `is_job_running(f"summarize_{docname}")`) to post the actual GL entries and closing balances and mark the PCV `gle_processing_status = "Completed"`. The `Paused`/`Cancelled` states (`pause_pcv_processing`, `cancel_pcv_processing`, `resume_pcv_processing`) integrate with the same state machine so paused/cancelled rows are never re-claimed. In short: a row is only ever handed to a worker if that worker's transaction can lock it while it's still `Queued` (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`), the row is atomically marked `Running` before the job runs, and the job verifies the `Running` status before doing any work — so no two workers can ever process the same date/report-type row.
